title: Barkman Avenue rebuilt as part of a long-term underground infrastructure renewal strategy
summary: Council gave first and second reading to a local improvement bylaw to replace the surface, water main and sewer main on three blocks of Barkman Avenue whose infrastructure had reached the end of its useful life. The mayor described it as part of a long-term strategy to renew underground infrastructure before it fails, with federal and provincial cost-sharing.
status_detail: The project was built in 2016; debt bylaw 2074 for the completed Barkman Avenue reconstruction was given readings on Dec 20, 2016.
figures: Total $2.14M: $1M borrowed over 5 years, $840,000 Canada-Manitoba Infrastructure Program, $300,000 Municipal Road Improvement Fund (transcript 2015-12-15 0:06:22)
public: One registered objection was on file (not read out).
mover: Michael Zwaagstra (first reading, as heard: 'Councilor Swiper')
notes: No written asset management plan was referred to; the 'strategy' is described verbally.

title: Council sets its direction in closed study sessions; no public strategic plan
summary: The mayor's New Year remarks (Jan 5, 2016) listed the year's priorities: multiplex plans, recreation and cultural facility renewal, infrastructure renewal and advocacy for personal care home beds. Council held a full-day summer study session on July 5, 2016 at the Mennonite Heritage Village on 'the big picture' and 'vision', and policy items were pre-discussed at the Strategic Priority Committee (SPC). None of these produced a written strategic plan or priorities document presented at a public meeting.
status_detail: No strategic plan, vision statement or published priorities list was tabled or adopted in public in Dec 2015 – Dec 2016. When a councillor referred to a study-session discussion in open council (Feb 2, 2016) the mayor asked her not to.
reasons: cost: Said council can only do so much: a set amount of time and set budget parameters limit what the vision can include (Jul 5, 2016). (Chris Goertzen)
notes: The Strategic Priority Committee is mentioned (Jun 21 and Oct 4, 2016) as where items were reviewed before council; its discussions are not in the videos.

title: Annual traffic study and a 'periphery road program', but no transportation master plan
summary: The city's 18th annual traffic study (Jan 5, 2016) showed traffic on PTH 12 and 52 rising about 2.5% a year and identified intersections needing work. The 2016 budget funded Old Tom Road paving under a boundary-road program and PTH 12 intersection work. Asked about Park Road West (Jun 7), staff said road upgrades are developer-driven and the right configuration was undetermined; the mayor said the city's share would be considered under the periphery road program and 'traffic management ideas'.
status_detail: Traffic study received as information; no transportation master plan or periphery road plan was tabled in this period.
figures: Average traffic growth about 2.5% a year (2016-01-05 0:04:00)
reasons: market-decides: Road and servicing improvements are normally developer-driven. (Troy Warkentin (staff))
notes: The councillor who asked about Park Road West on Jun 7 is not named in the recording.

title: City signs new Dutch elm disease cost-sharing deal despite provincial download
summary: The province changed the Dutch elm disease control program so municipalities pay to remove diseased trees. Council signed the new agreement to protect the city's elms, at an expected extra net cost of about $20,000 a year, and agreed to send the Minister of Conservation a letter of frustration.
status_detail: Agreement approved; letter to the minister agreed by consensus.
figures: About $20,000 a year net extra cost (2016-01-19 0:16:46)
reasons: provincial-responsibility: The province transferred operating dollars but not the capital costs of the program. (Chris Goertzen)
seconder: Councillor Penner (which Penner not stated; heard as 'Kenner')
notes: Same Jan 19 meeting: letters confirming the province's $5 million commitment to the first phase of recreation and cultural facilities were taken as information.

title: City seeks federal and provincial money for a performing arts centre under its $7.5M cap
summary: Following the July 2015 resolution capping the city's share at $7.5 million (and not proceeding until other funding was confirmed), the province's $5 million commitment letter was received (Jan 19, 2016). Administration flagged the federal Canada Cultural Spaces Fund (May 17) and council approved a Small Communities Fund application for a $22.5 million project asking $7.5 million each from Ottawa and the province (Sep 6). A $24.3 million Class C estimate later became public in the media.
status_detail: Applications submitted; no federal or matching provincial approval announced at council by Dec 2016.
figures: City cap $7.5M; application total $22.5M with $7.5M federal + $7.5M provincial requested (transcript 2016-09-06 1:20:56); Class C estimate $24.3M (2016-12-20)
reasons: waiting-for-funding: Recreation planning and the arts centre clearly need support from other levels of government. (Michael Zwaagstra)
notes: Mover on Sep 6 is not named in the recording.

title: Friendly annexation of land from the RM of Hanover still in progress
summary: A 'friendly annexation' agreement with the RM of Hanover, negotiated through the Steinbach–Hanover Joint Action Committee led by Councillor Siemens, was in progress. Land from an earlier annexation was being developed (Lexington Village, Jul 19), the city set aside $50,000 for a future tax-sharing payment to Hanover, and staff said the annexed area would need a zoning review within up to 24 months of provincial approval. At the Nov 1 organizational meeting the mayor reappointed Siemens to finish the agreement.
status_detail: Agreement 'not complete yet' as of Nov 1, 2016; awaiting provincial approval. Correspondence 'in regards to annexation' was taken as information Sep 6, 2016 without discussion.
figures: $50,000 to committed expenditure reserve for future tax-sharing payment to RM of Hanover (2016-03-15 0:45:50); zoning review of new area up to 24 months (2016-11-01 0:16:35)
notes: The size of the area, provincial application date and agreement terms were not stated at council in this period.

title: Residents' request for a sidewalk with Old Tom Road paving deferred to a future sidewalk plan
summary: Residents on Lyons Gate wrote asking for a sidewalk with the Old Tom Road paving. Staff estimated $700,000–$800,000, roughly doubling the project. Councillors agreed to keep paving and sidewalks separate and consider the request in an overall sidewalk/pathway discussion; the mayor said regional pathways could be considered as the friendly annexation added land east of the road.
status_detail: Taken as information; deferred to a future sidewalk plan discussion. No active transportation plan was tabled in this period.
figures: Sidewalk estimate $700,000–$800,000 vs $1M budgeted for the road project (2016-02-02 1:19:50)
reasons: cost: Would virtually double the paving budget. (John Fehr); one-step-at-a-time: Focus on the roadway first; pathways are a separate, bigger consultation. (Jac Siemens)
public: A Lyons Gate household (T.) asked for a sidewalk along Old Tom Road.
notes: The cost and doubling remark at 1:22:20 is by a speaker introduced as 'Councilor Kerrio' (identity uncertain; Cari Penner was excused that night), so it is not quoted.

title: City Hall addition built after years of delay
summary: Council awarded the City Hall addition tender to Penco Construction for about $1.44 million, under budget. Councillors said it had been delayed several times for lack of funds; the mayor recalled discussing it 7 or 8 years earlier.
status_detail: Tender awarded Jun 21, 2016; construction expected to start mid-July 2016.
reasons: cost: Delayed several times because council felt it did not have the funds. (John Fehr)

title: 2016 financial plan adopted with a 4-year capital outlook
summary: The 2016 financial plan (public hearing Feb 16, 2016) set a $12.9 million capital program, $150,000 for engineering studies for future water and well supply, and a forward capital outlook of $17.4 million for 2017 (including the Performing Arts Centre building and a water supply expansion), then $18.9M, $7.2M and $4.6M for the following three years. Treasurer Brian Hrehirchuk said debt payments were projected to rise with the city's growth. Council adopted it in principle on Feb 16 and formally on Apr 5, 2016.
status_detail: Adopted in principle Feb 16, 2016 (moved by Councillor Zwaagstra) and given formal adoption on Apr 5, 2016 once school tax figures were in.
figures: Mill rate 13.23 (down 1.07); capital program $12.9M; $150,000 engineering studies for future water and well supply; 2017 program $17.4M; then $18.9M, $7.2M, $4.6M; debt to be $7.6M end-2016 on 5-year amortization; 24 single-family permits in 2015 (transcript, financial plan hearing 0:01:21)
reasons: cost: Net-zero tax budget that still takes care of basic infrastructure. (Michael Zwaagstra)
public: No member of the public spoke at the hearing.
notes: Seconder not audible in the recording.

title: City does not object to an RM of La Broquerie zoning change; transition zone agreement unaffected
summary: Administration reviewed a zoning bylaw amendment by the neighbouring RM of La Broquerie and recommended no objection. The mayor confirmed the separate transition zone agreement between the city and the RM, which sits in the RM's development plan, was not affected.
status_detail: No objection filed; no motion needed.
notes: 'Arm of Le Broquerie' is the transcript's rendering of 'RM of La Broquerie'.

title: Design of a new well field and water supply plant started; funding sought
summary: After three years of aquifer testing for quality and capacity, council awarded AECOM the design of a water supply expansion with a plant expected near Park Road West in the northwest of the city (Jun 21, 2016). It then applied for federal and provincial funding (Sep 6) and passed the resolution needed for the Clean Water and Wastewater Fund (Oct 18). Councillor Zwaagstra framed it as supply for the medium and long-term future; the mayor said it would add capacity for an expanding city.
status_detail: Design contract awarded and funding applications filed; construction depended on the grants and had not started by Dec 2016.
figures: AECOM design $350,470 + $7,510 expenses (2016-06-21 0:03:39); project $10M, federal up to $5M, provincial up to $2.5M, city $2.5M (2016-09-06 1:23:21; 2016-10-18 1:28:52)
reasons: waiting-for-funding: The project can only proceed with partnerships. (Michael Zwaagstra)
mover: Michael Zwaagstra (Jun 21, Oct 18); Councillor Penner (Sep 6, which Penner not stated)
notes: Wastewater treatment/lagoon capacity was not discussed at council in this period.

title: Task force reports public survey on recreation and cultural facilities
summary: The Task Force on Public Engagement for Recreation and Cultural Facilities (Councillors Susan Penner, Cari Penner and Michael Zwaagstra) reported a random telephone poll of 500 people plus online public and business consultations. It recommended not proceeding until the announced $5 million provincial funding was confirmed, pursuing federal funding, raising 10% privately, building downtown only if parking is solved, and adding day-to-day space if affordable. The mayor said the data should culminate in a master plan.
status_detail: Report received and results posted on the city website; its recommendations were folded into the Apr 5, 2016 principles.
figures: 500-person random telephone poll; arts centre business plan showed $500,000–$600,000 annual operating deficit (transcript 2016-03-15 0:26:16, 0:38:41)
reasons: waiting-for-funding: Provincial $5M must be confirmed — 'a deal breaker'. (Susan Penner)
public: Residents valued arts and culture, preferred downtown, but raised parking and operating-cost concerns (as summarized by the task force).

title: City keeps buying downtown lots near the arenas for future facilities and parking
summary: Continuing a 15–20-year strategy to assemble land around the T.G. Smith Centre/arenas for future recreation facilities, parking or other municipal uses, council bought four residential properties in 2016: 376 Hanover St (Apr 5), 385 Elmdale St (Sep 20, completing the Elmdale frontage), 316 Hanover St (Oct 18) and 326 Hanover St (Nov 1). Councillor Siemens objected to the April purchase because there was no plan for the land.
status_detail: All four purchases approved, funded from the general operating fund and reserves; houses to be rented until the land is used. No plan for the assembled land was adopted in the period.
mover: Councillor Penner (Apr 5 and Oct 18, which Penner not stated); Michael Zwaagstra (Sep 20, Nov 1)
vote: all carried; Apr 5 opposed by Siemens (count not recorded)
notes: Mayor and staff variously describe the program as 15 or 20 years old.

title: Council drops the multiplex and adopts five principles for future recreation planning
summary: Councillor Susan Penner moved, and Councillor Zwaagstra seconded, that the city recognize a multiplex is not financially feasible; keep planning a downtown performing arts centre only with adequate parking, other-government funding and at least 10% private fundraising; look to secure land for a future spectator arena outside downtown; and keep dedicating 1.241 mills to the recreation reserve. Mayor Goertzen argued against, saying council was abandoning a master plan near the finish line just as federal infrastructure money was opening up.
status_detail: Carried 5-2 (Goertzen and Fehr against, per SteinbachOnline; the video ends before the vote). The arena-land principle had no follow-up purchase in 2016; the city's downtown land buying continued.
figures: MNP 2012 multiplex estimate over $100M; Stantec 2014/15 about $71M; city tax revenue about $13M/yr; recreation reserve 1.241 mills (about $1.1M/yr) (transcript 2016-04-05 part 2, 0:46:46 and 0:50:47)
reasons: cost: A city taking in $13M a year in taxes cannot afford a $71M–$100M multiplex without massive tax increases. (Susan Penner); waiting-for-funding: Two-thirds funding from other governments is unrealistic; even then $33M of borrowing would need a tax increase. (Michael Zwaagstra); one-step-at-a-time: Phase recreation projects within what the city can afford instead of one large building. (Michael Zwaagstra)
public: The task force survey (Mar 15) found residents preferred a downtown arts centre but worried about parking. The Steinbach Arts Council sent a letter (taken as information).
decision_source: transcript (motion and debate); vote count from SteinbachOnline
notes: The video ends during debate, before the vote; result and count (5-2, Goertzen and Fehr against) are from SteinbachOnline ('A complex history of Steinbach's multiplex'; 'Penner wants to drop arts centre plan', Dec 20, 2016). Siemens's and Cari Penner's votes are inferred from that count.

title: One-time relaxation of city servicing standards for a highway commercial subdivision
summary: A developer of the Steinbach North C-3 subdivision asked to use swale drainage without curb and gutter instead of the city's construction specification. Councillor Siemens moved approval through a development agreement, arguing the city's industrial parks had largely sat empty and it needed employers; Cari Penner seconded. Councillor Zwaagstra and the city manager warned it would set a precedent for commercial servicing standards across the city.
status_detail: Carried (Deputy Mayor Fehr chairing) as a one-time exception: gravity sewer, piped water, 32-foot concrete street, swale drainage, no curb and gutter. No change to the city specification.
reasons: market-decides: A private developer building at its own cost should be accommodated to attract employers. (Jac Siemens)
public: The developer's representatives said city servicing conditions caused buyer resistance (Apr 5 and May 3).
vote: carried; Zwaagstra stated he would vote against (count not recorded)
notes: Borderline for this topic: an individual development, included because council debated city-wide servicing standards and industrial growth.

title: New water and sewer rates sent to the Public Utilities Board to fund operations and future upgrades
summary: Council gave first reading to water and wastewater rate bylaw 2064 after a rate study, with increases of about 3%, and sent it to the Public Utilities Board. Councillor Zwaagstra said rates must cover operations and future upgrades; the mayor said regular reviews avoid large catch-up increases.
status_detail: First reading only; PUB review and final readings not seen at council in this period.
figures: Increases about 3% (2016-05-17 0:06:18); 2016 budget had water +4.8%, sewer +1.6% (financial plan hearing)

title: Golf club asks for a drainage partnership as development sends more runoff its way
summary: The golf club board told council (Jul 5, 2016) that development in and around Steinbach, plus the diversion of the Elmdale Drain, had increased water flowing onto the course. It asked for an active partnership, compensation for losses (about $48,000 a year), future funding if damage recurs, and a $50,000 annual recreation grant. Staff said new subdivisions must hold outflow to pre-development levels (provincial rule). Councillor Fehr, the conservation district representative, said talks on upstream retention had stalled.
status_detail: The mayor said the requests would be dealt with in the budget process ending in November; no decision was reported at council in this period.
figures: Lost revenue about $48,000/yr from closures vs about $23,500 in 2000; requested $50,000/yr recreation grant (2016-07-05 0:35:12, 0:36:01)
reasons: provincial-responsibility: The drain through the course is a provincial drain; asked whether the province should contribute. (John Fehr); neighbours-disagree: Much of the water originates in the adjoining municipality; needs partnerships across boundaries. (Chris Goertzen)
public: B.S., for the golf club board: development has changed how water flows and the club cannot afford the infrastructure to handle it alone.
notes: The city had no stormwater master plan referenced in this period.

title: Councillor Susan Penner asks whether the city can partner with surrounding RMs on regional facilities
summary: In her Sep 20, 2016 opening, Councillor Susan Penner said Steinbach (about 15,000 people) serves a region of 30,000–60,000, that growth costs money, and that city taxpayers cover operating deficits of facilities like the aquatic centre that are mostly used by non-residents. She asked whether the city could partner with surrounding RMs on regional facilities.
status_detail: No motion or follow-up on regional facility cost-sharing was recorded in this period.
figures: Population about 15,000; trading area 30,000–60,000 (2016-09-20 0:00:01)
reasons: cost: Steinbach's tax base is much smaller than the region it serves; residents carry facility deficits. (Susan Penner)

title: Growth-pays fees renewed for 2017–2019 at 2.5% a year
summary: Council renewed the residential (Bylaw 2070) and non-residential (Bylaw 2071) capital development fee schedules for three years to the end of 2019, with 2.5% annual increases, after review at the Strategic Priority Committee. The fees fund sidewalks in new neighbourhoods, transportation upgrades, fire services and other growth-related infrastructure.
status_detail: First reading Oct 4; second and third readings Nov 1, 2016.
figures: 2.5% annual increase to end of 2019; 2016 budget expected $769,000 in capital development fees (transcript 2016-10-04 0:09:24; financial plan hearing 0:01:21)
reasons: cost: Keep increases near inflation so fees stay affordable. (Michael Zwaagstra)
public: The Haven Group asked for a development fee rebate for 55+ housing (Oct 4); council asked it to clarify whether the project was supportive housing.
seconder: Councillor Penner (2070, which Penner not stated), Jac Siemens (2071)
notes: No growth study or capital plan was cited to set the fee levels; increases tracked inflation.

title: Secondary plan amended to reserve a future school site on the west side
summary: Council amended the Park Hill secondary plan (Bylaw 2072) and rezoned land to educational institutional (Bylaw 2073) to create a future school site for the Hanover School Division along McKenzie Avenue. The mayor stressed that secondary plans are long-term concept plans and that a school depends on provincial funding.
status_detail: First readings Oct 18; public hearing with no objections and second and third readings Dec 20, 2016, plus the subdivision and road opening for Parkland Drive.
reasons: provincial-responsibility: Schools are determined by provincial funding; the site is not a promise of a school. (Chris Goertzen)
public: The developer's representative said the site was designed to Hanover School Division needs.
mover: Michael Zwaagstra (Bylaw 2072 first reading); Cari Penner (second reading Dec 20)
notes: Zwaagstra's Oct 18 remark is transcribed 'as climate continues to grow' (likely 'as the city continues to grow'), so it is not quoted. The Dec 20 second-reading mover is the Penner who seconded the arts centre motion (Cari Penner).

title: Split council reaffirms $7.5M arts centre commitment with a June 30, 2017 deadline
summary: After a $24.3 million Class C estimate was reported in the media and some councillors spoke publicly against the project, the mayor asked council to honour its earlier votes. Deputy Mayor John Fehr moved to reaffirm the $7.5 million commitment, conditional on other funding, with a sunset of June 30, 2017; Councillor Cari Penner seconded. Zwaagstra, Susan Penner and Funk opposed, saying the project had grown from about $15 million to $24.3 million and had never been voted on at that size.
status_detail: Carried 4-3. The commitment would lapse if funding was not in place by June 30, 2017 (outcome falls outside this period).
figures: City share $7.5M (unchanged); Class C estimate $24.3M vs earlier outer limit about $15M (transcript 2016-12-20 0:44:53)
reasons: cost: Estimate about 60% above the outer limit council had when it voted; new information justifies a different decision. (Michael Zwaagstra); cost: The project went from $15M to $24M. (Susan Penner)
decision_source: transcript; names of opponents confirmed by SteinbachOnline Dec 20, 2016
notes: Siemens's vote is inferred from the 4-3 count (the three opponents are named by SteinbachOnline). Speaker I at 0:50:01 (probably Siemens) supported the motion but is not named in the recording.

title: Annual budgets carry only a short capital look-ahead and 5-year debt policy
summary: Each financial plan ended with a short 'longer-term overview': four future years of capital totals with few named projects. Council relied on reserves (capital development, utility replacement, recreation) and a policy of repaying all debt within 5 years. The 2018 look-ahead named infrastructure renewal, equipment and cemetery expansion, not wastewater.
status_detail: 2017 and 2018 financial plans adopted (2018: R18-056, 4-3 over taxes). No long-range (10–20 year) capital plan was presented in public.
figures: 2017 plan: 2018 $23.7M, then $6.3M, $7.1M, $4M (2017 FPH 0:00:49). 2018 plan: 2019 $6.6M, then $5.7M, $5M, $8M (2018 FPH 0:00:58). 2018 reserve transfers: $300,000 to capital development, $550,000 utility replacement, >$1M recreation (2018-03-20 0:29:58, 0:33:16, 0:34:03).
reasons: cost: 5-year debt policy keeps borrowing short and frees capacity for later projects. (Michael Zwaagstra)
vote: 2018: 4-3 (against: Zwaagstra, S. Penner, Funk) — tax dispute; 2017: carried, not recorded
notes: The 2018 financial plan split was over the tax increase (covered by the taxes report), so it is not listed in split_votes here.

title: City sells its own industrial lots and buys one back; industrial park 'filling up'
summary: The city develops and sells industrial lots with build-within deadlines. In Feb 2017 council used a buy-back clause to repurchase 88 Acres Drive ($49,300) over Councillor Zwaagstra's objection that the city already had enough industrial inventory; it sold 127 Industrial Road ($75,000, 2017 offer and 2018 sale); and in June 2018 the Steinbach Community Development Corporation subdivided 4.5 acres in the industrial park for buyers. The mayor noted the park was 'filling up'. No new industrial land plan was discussed.
status_detail: Buy-back and sales carried; R18-109 (sale of 127 Industrial Road to Hidjak Ltd., May 15, 2018) unanimous. No plan for the next industrial area came to council in 2017–2018.
figures: 88 Acres Drive buy-back $49,300 at 85% of original price (2017-02-21 0:37:03); 127 Industrial Road $75,000 (2017-05-16 0:17:00; R18-109); incubator lots ~$75,000 (2018-06-05 0:20:20); SCDC subdivision of ~4.5 acres into two 2-acre parcels (2018-06-19 0:45:26).
reasons: market-decides: Opposed adding to city-held industrial inventory; owner free to sell privately. (Michael Zwaagstra)
vote: unanimous (2018); 2017 buy-back carried, vote not recorded

title: $24M performing arts centre dropped after missing its funding deadline; promised recreation/culture consultation not seen
summary: The 2017 financial plan carried a $24M Performing Arts Centre ($12M in 2017, $12M in 2018; city commitment $7.5M). Councillors Zwaagstra and Funk voted against the budget because of it. When the June 30, 2017 deadline passed without full funding, Mayor Goertzen announced the project would not proceed in its present form and promised consultations on future recreation and cultural plans, with over $1M kept in a reserve.
status_detail: Project ended July 4, 2017. No public consultation on future recreation/culture plans appeared in 2017–2018 council meetings; the 2018 budget had no new recreation or arts facility (Siemens). Recreation reserve grew by over $1M in 2018 (mayor, 2018-03-20).
figures: $24M total; $12M/yr 2017–2018; $2.5M borrowing in 2017 (Zwaagstra, 2017 FPH 0:16:03); city's earlier commitment $7.5M (2017 FPH 0:20:14); 2017 capital program $24.6M (Hrehirchuk).
reasons: waiting-for-funding: Funding deadline missed, so the project would not move forward. (Chris Goertzen); cost: Project 'dwarfs all of the other capital plans'. (Michael Zwaagstra); cost: Warned against heading down the road of borrowing. (Earl Funk)
vote: 2017 financial plan carried; Zwaagstra and Funk stated they would vote against (not recorded)
notes: The PAC's earlier approvals (2016) fall outside this period.

title: Second water supply system (new wells and water treatment plant) approved, funded and built for growth
summary: Council carried an ~$11M supplementary water supply project (new wells, treatment, storage and pumping on Park Road West) through a local improvement by-law in 2017, resubmitted its federal Clean Water and Wastewater Fund application to get a larger share covered, awarded the construction tender in February 2018 with a reduced scope to stay within funding, and passed the debt by-law in December 2018. Members repeatedly described it as the infrastructure the city needs to keep growing.
status_detail: Tender awarded Feb 20, 2018 (R18-032); plant under construction in 2018 (city building permit of $10,589,000 noted Nov 20, 2018); debt issue By-law 2114 given first and second reading Dec 18, 2018 (R18-297, R18-298); land for the plant bought from the Steinbach Community Development Corporation for $1 (R18-287).
figures: Project ~$11M, debt up to $5.375M under Local Improvement By-law 2085 (transcript 2017-07-04 0:09:26; 2017-09-19 0:26:38); CWWF first approved for only a $2.5M portion, resubmitted as a $10M project (2017-08-01 0:14:20); tender low bid $11,342,984.22, awarded at $10,589,192.59 after $753,791.63 of deletions plus $230,000 utility reserve and $414,000 utility surplus (2018-02-20 0:08:47; minutes R18-032); $5.6M from other governments (mayor, 2018-02-20 0:11:25); AECOM construction administration $780,000 (R18-017); 2018 capital program $17.2M, 'majority' for this project (2018 financial plan hearing 0:00:58).
reasons: waiting-for-funding: Passed the borrowing by-law but said the city would wait for federal/provincial dollars before proceeding (2017-07-04, 2017-09-19). (Chris Goertzen); cost: Stressed the 5-year debt policy and that budgeting would offset the 1.41-mill isolated impact so taxes need not rise. (Michael Zwaagstra)
public: Two notices of objection were received at the July 4, 2017 local improvement hearing, one raising tax concerns (writers not named here).
decision_source: minutes (2018); transcript for 2017 readings of By-law 2085 (carried, no recorded opposition)
notes: 2017 readings of By-law 2085 and the CWWF resolutions are from transcripts only (no 2017 minutes). The CM's Feb 2018 report and the 2018 hearing call it a 'water treatment plant'/'water treatment facility'.

title: City Manager reports ~4% annual growth for 20 years; no formal population forecast debated
summary: The City Manager's first annual report in some years (Feb 6, 2018) said Steinbach had averaged just under 4% growth a year for 20 years and expected that to continue. Asked by Councillor Zwaagstra what population threshold would next change how the city works, he declined to speculate. The only explicit projection in the period came from the province: the OCP 'anticipates' 25,000 residents within 10 years.
status_detail: Received as information; council did not discuss or adopt a population forecast or growth-management strategy in 2017–2018.
figures: Growth just under 4%/yr over 20 years vs just over 1% for Manitoba (CM, 2018-02-06 0:04:58); 2016 census 'just under 16,000' (Zwaagstra, 0:19:12); population passed 15,000, raising the city's RCMP share from 70% to 90% (2017 and 2018 financial plan hearings); OCP anticipates 25,000 in 10 years (provincial planner, 2018-07-17 0:45:45); 233 residential units / ~$57M permits in 2017 (CM).
reasons: growth-unpredictable: 'Without having had a chance to consider it thoughtfully, I won't speculate'; said the city would try to 'stay ahead of the curve'. (Troy Warkentin)
notes: The 25,000 figure is the provincial reviewer's reading of the OCP; the OCP text itself was not checked.

title: Defending the transition zone with La Broquerie: objections and a new joint action committee
summary: Council objected in March 2017 to a La Broquerie rezoning just outside the city that it said breached the transition zone and duty to consult, sending staff to the Municipal Board. After La Broquerie complained, Mayor Goertzen and the Reeve agreed in Oct 2017 to form a joint action committee, created in Nov 2017. In Aug 2018 council objected to La Broquerie's new development plan and zoning by-law, which proposed removing the transitional policy area.
status_detail: Joint action committee formed Nov 7, 2017 (Goertzen, Fehr) and continued by the new council (Bill Hiebert, Nov 6, 2018); objections filed (R18-175, R18-176). Outcome of the 2017 Municipal Board hearing and of La Broquerie's 2018 plan not found in council records.
reasons: neighbours-disagree: Transition policy is 'a good tool for us to continue to work together'; objection is the formal route when the neighbour departs from it. (Chris Goertzen)
mover: Michael Zwaagstra (2017-03-21); Cari Penner (R18-175); Jac Siemens (R18-176)
seconder: Councillor Penner (2017, unidentified); Michael Zwaagstra (R18-175); Susan Penner (R18-176)

title: Decades-long downtown land assembly near the arenas and T.G. Smith Centre continued over one councillor's objection
summary: Council kept buying houses near the arenas, curling rink and T.G. Smith Centre (Barkman Ave, Hanover St) under a land-assembly strategy staff dated back 20–25 years, so a large downtown block would be available for a future use (recreation, parking, multi-family, mixed use, a hotel). No use was decided; supporters said the next council could start planning it. Councillor Fehr voted against each 2018 purchase, saying it pushed residents and businesses out and overspent the land budget.
status_detail: Land acquired (316 Barkman 2017; 336, 332 and 380 Hanover St in 2018); the CM said this completed 'most' of the block, but no plan for its use was adopted in 2017–2018.
reasons: market-decides: Opposed buying: drives residents and would-be businesses out of downtown, parking already shared, no public support heard, budget exceeded. (John Fehr)
notes: The 2017 Barkman purchase vote is from the transcript (carried; mover a Councillor Penner, seconder Siemens). The CM confirmed (minutes 2018-08-21, item 19.1) houses are rented, demolished or moved depending on condition.

title: Annexation of just under 3,000 acres from the RM of Hanover approved in part, effective Jan 1, 2018
summary: The city's multi-year annexation application concluded in 2017 when the Municipal Board and the Province approved part of it, adding just under 3,000 acres (2,795 acres by Councillor Siemens' count) from the RM of Hanover, effective January 1, 2018. The City Manager said the approval was less than the city requested and less than its projected growth rates called for. Council then updated the OCP, zoning by-law, road names, emergency plan and servicing for the new area.
status_detail: Approved in part (smaller than requested); in effect Jan 1, 2018. Follow-up: OCP By-law 2099 and Zoning By-law 2100 (third readings Oct 16, 2018), road renaming By-law 2098 (Aug 2018), emergency plan amendments (R18-028), ~11 miles of gravel roads added to public works and solid waste routes.
figures: Just under 3,000 acres (CM, 2018-02-06 0:04:58); 2,795 acres (Siemens, 2018-10-16 0:00:23); ~11 miles of gravel roads added (CM); annexation effective Jan 1, 2018 (minutes 2018-12-04).
public: A resident of the annexed area (E.P., Dec 4, 2018) said residents were told at annexation meetings they would get garbage and recycling pickup but received no notice for most of 2018 (her account; not verified). A farmer (M.R.) speaking for the Manitoba Turkey Board urged protection of productive farmland in the annexed Development Reserve 2 area (July 17, 2018).
decision_source: transcript (Municipal Board and provincial approval; no council resolution in the period)
notes: The annexation application, Municipal Board hearings and provincial order were not debated in the council transcripts available (2017-04-04 and 2017-10-17 videos are missing). The CM mentions the city reopened the hearing with an alternate proposal. Acreage figures differ slightly between speakers.

title: New Official Community Plan (By-law 2099) adopted early to cover annexed land
summary: Prompted by the annexation, council applied in Sept 2017 for a provincial grant (up to 50%) to review its OCP and zoning by-law, held open houses, reviewed drafts at the Strategic Priorities Committee (Mar 27, 2018), and adopted By-law 2099 in Oct 2018. Changes were almost entirely limited to the annexed land (new Development Reserve 1 and 2 designations letting agriculture continue). Council rejected a resident's request to leave the plan to the next council.
status_detail: Grant approved under Manitoba's Community Planning Assistance Program (minutes 2018-01-16, item 19); first reading May 15, 2018 (R18-116); public hearing and second reading July 17, 2018 (transcript, carried); ministerial approval; third reading Oct 16, 2018 (R18-242, unanimous).
figures: Provincial grant up to 50% of cost (2017-09-19 0:17:41); OCP last reviewed 2015, review required at least every 5 years (CM, 2018-05-15 0:32:59; 2018-07-17 0:15:15).
reasons: one-step-at-a-time: Called the OCP 'specifically a 5-year planning document' and said the changes were limited to the annexed areas, the rest having been approved by the province in 2015. (Michael Zwaagstra); already-planned: Said questions from provincial Community and Regional Planning had been answered by staff. (Michael Zwaagstra)
public: T.B. (resident) asked council to delay second reading until the new council and raised gaps in green space, affordability and the First Street transitional zone. M.R. (farmer, speaking for the Manitoba Turkey Board) said Development Reserve 2 is some of Manitoba's most productive farmland and asked for infill-first and protection for livestock operations. G.C. and K.L. (residents) spoke on the separate 80 Brandt Street OCP amendment in Dec 2017.
mover: John Fehr (R18-116); Michael Zwaagstra (R18-242; also moved 2nd reading Jul 17)
decision_source: minutes (1st, 3rd); transcript (2nd reading, 2018-07-17, no minutes available)
notes: No minutes for July 17, 2018 in the downloads; second reading is from the transcript. The provincial grant amount actually received was not found.

title: New Zoning By-law 2100 adopted; downtown parking review left to the next council
summary: A rewritten zoning by-law, again driven by the annexation, went through committee, an open house, first reading (June 5, 2018, after a divided vote on hard-surfacing rules), a July 17 public hearing and third reading on Oct 16, 2018. Councillor Siemens and others said downtown (CBD) parking requirements were too restrictive and asked a future council to review them.
status_detail: Third reading Oct 16, 2018 (R18-243, unanimous). The CBD parking review Siemens asked for was left to the next council; no result in 2018.
reasons: one-step-at-a-time: Voted to pass the by-law now and review downtown parking after, rather than delay the whole by-law. (Jac Siemens)
public: Residents raised numbering/reference errors and First Street concerns at the July 17 hearing (T.B. and others); the provincial planner suggested delegating 15% minor variances.
vote: unanimous on readings; surfacing amendment R18-128 carried 4-2 (against: Goertzen, C. Penner)
notes: Second reading on July 17, 2018 is from the transcript (no minutes).

title: OCP redesignation on Brandt Street denied pending the 2018 plan review
summary: Council denied an OCP amendment (By-law 2087) to redesignate 80 Brandt Street from residential to commercial for an Envision office, though members liked the use. Councillor Siemens said the long-term designation of the whole area should be considered in the 2018 OCP review rather than at a single meeting.
status_detail: Amendment denied Dec 5, 2017; rezoning hearing cancelled. The 2018 OCP (By-law 2099) changed almost nothing outside the annexed lands, so the area-wide review Siemens described did not happen in 2018.
reasons: study-first: Review the whole area in the 2018 OCP review, not one property. (Jac Siemens)
public: K.L. (resident, 45 years on Brandt Street) objected to commercial creep on the block; G.C. (property owner) supported the change, citing a future city of '25,000, 30,000, 40,000 people'.
notes: Included because council debated long-term land use policy through this application.

title: Federal gas-tax deadline for an asset management plan noted; no plan presented
summary: In Nov 2017 the City Manager reported that under the federal gas tax agreement Manitoba municipalities had to work toward asset management plans by March 31, 2018; the provincial template was delayed and the city would file a progress report by Dec 15, 2017. Council took it as information.
status_detail: Received as information. No asset management plan or policy came to council in public in 2017–2018.
figures: Deadline March 31, 2018; progress report due Dec 15, 2017 (CM, 0:31:10).
reasons: provincial-responsibility: Provincial model and reporting template delayed. (Troy Warkentin)

title: 40 acres bought from the Fly-In Golf Club for $500,000 and leased back for $1 a year
summary: After declining a $500,000 grant request from the Steinbach Fly-In Golf Club, council (in closed meetings) negotiated to buy 40 acres of the course for $500,000 over 3 years and lease it back for $1/year to about 2083. Supporters called it land banking for the city's future (it adjoins 40 city-owned acres and could join A.D. Penner Park or be sold for development). Opponents called it a bailout dressed as a land deal, noted there was no appraisal, and said the city controls zoning without owning the land.
status_detail: Purchase and lease both carried Dec 5, 2017 (votes not recorded; positions stated imply 4-3). Possession March 1, 2018.
figures: $500,000 for 40 acres, paid over 3 years (~$167,000/yr) to avoid a debenture (Zwaagstra, 1:07:55); lease $1/yr to ~2083 (~63 years) (CM, 0:58:52); land budget $300,000/yr (Fehr, 1:01:04); members claimed value 'upwards of $1 million' if not landlocked (Fehr; a Councillor Penner) — no appraisal tabled.
reasons: cost: Half a million tax dollars to keep the course operating; restructured to 3 years to avoid Municipal Board scrutiny. (Michael Zwaagstra); not-council-role: City does not need to own land to control its use; a bailout benefiting the course and its lender. (Earl Funk)
public: No public input: Zwaagstra and Funk said a closed-meeting motion to have the golf club present publicly was defeated 4-3 (their account).
vote: carried; not recorded (stated: for Fehr, Siemens, Goertzen, one Councillor Penner; against Zwaagstra, Funk, the other Councillor Penner)
notes: No 2017 minutes; the 4-3 split is inferred from members' stated intentions and the 'defeated 4-3' references. Which Councillor Penner voted which way could not be confirmed (one, transcript label J, argued it was a disguised operating grant; the other, label M, called it a win-win aligned with the OCP's parks vision).

title: Lagoon expansion named the 'next major hurdle' for growth, but no plan or study started
summary: During the City Manager's 2017 annual report, Mayor Goertzen said the next major hurdle would likely be expanding the sewage lagoon. The City Manager said the 2007 lagoon expansion gave the city 'about a dozen to 20 years of capacity' and that it was something to 'be aware of and work towards'. No wastewater study, capital line or timeline followed in 2017–2018.
status_detail: Received as information. The 2018 financial plan's four-year capital look-ahead ($6.6M, $5.7M, $5M, $8M) did not mention the lagoon; no wastewater planning item came to council in 2017–2018.
figures: Last lagoon expansion completed 2007, 'about a dozen to 20 years of capacity' i.e. roughly 2019–2027 (CM, 2018-02-06 0:21:43).
reasons: growth-unpredictable: Would not speculate on the next growth threshold; said Steinbach was entering 'uncharted territory' in Manitoba. (Troy Warkentin)
notes: The capacity window (to roughly 2019–2027) is the City Manager's off-the-cuff estimate, not a study.

title: Arts Centre building repair matched ($65,000) after being tabled 4-3
summary: With no new recreation or culture facility in sight after the PAC, Councillor Susan Penner moved to match a $65,000 Co-op grant to repair the 84-year-old city-owned Arts Centre building from the recreation and culture reserve, saying larger projects had been 'too large in scope for our city'. Council tabled it 4-3 in June over administration's questions, then approved a revised matching motion in September.
status_detail: Tabled June 19, 2018 (R18-148, 4-3); $65,000 match approved Sept 4, 2018 (R18-205, S. Penner/C. Penner, unanimous).
figures: $65,000 Co-op Community Spaces grant matched by $65,000 from the Recreation and Culture reserve (minutes 2018-06-19, 2018-09-04).
reasons: study-first: Questions from administration about the plans and the lease needed answers first. (Chris Goertzen)
public: The Steinbach Arts Council had told council in Oct 2017 that its building urgently needed improvements (per the motion).
mover: Susan Penner (motion); John Fehr (R18-148 to table)
vote: R18-148 4-3 (against tabling: S. Penner, C. Penner, Funk); R18-205 unanimous
notes: A repair rather than a long-range facility; included because it shows how council handled facility needs after the PAC.

title: Objection to the RM of Hanover's development plan, withdrawn after Hanover changed it
summary: In June 2018 council objected to Hanover's proposed Development Plan By-law 2417-18 because it allowed fringe development incompatible with an urban centre and without urban servicing standards. After meetings of administrations and the Hanover-Steinbach joint task force, Hanover changed policies for the transitional area around the city (land the city had failed to annex), dropped a proposed rural business area and adjusted AG-2 uses; council withdrew its objection in October.
status_detail: Objection R18-138 (June 19, 2018); objection withdrawn R18-235 (Oct 2, 2018) after Hanover's amendments.
reasons: neighbours-disagree: Fringe development and lack of urban servicing standards could impair long-term land use sustainability (minutes 2018-06-19, item 18). (Troy Warkentin)
notes: A Hanover–Steinbach joint council meeting was planned for Dec 6, 2018 (mentioned 2018-12-04); its content is not in the record.

title: PTH 12/52 highway access plan referenced and road widenings secured; no city transportation plan
summary: A PTH 12 / PTH 52 Highway Access Management and Transportation Plan study was completed in 2017 and referenced in the new OCP, but the city would not adopt it until Manitoba Infrastructure did. Council used development applications to secure land for future intersection upgrades (Lowen Blvd at PTH 12, By-law 2104, Aug 2018), calling it long-term planning; a new PTH 12 turning lane followed the access plan.
status_detail: Road widening By-law 2104 passed (first reading Aug 7, second and third Aug 21, 2018; R18-181, R18-189, R18-190). The access plan awaited Manitoba Infrastructure adoption; the CM said the McKenzie/Brandt eastbound lane was built per the plan (minutes 2018-09-18, item 23.1). No city-wide transportation plan was started.
reasons: provincial-responsibility: City will not adopt the highway access plan until Manitoba Infrastructure formally adopts it. (Lacey Gaudet (City Planner))
seconder: Cari Penner (1st); Michael Zwaagstra (2nd); Jac Siemens (3rd)
notes: The 'PTH-2' in the transcript is likely PTH 52 (the minutes say PTH 12 plan). Bypass not discussed in this period.

title: Province urges climate (GHG) planning and early transit planning; city defers
summary: At the July 17, 2018 OCP hearing, Manitoba's Community and Regional Planning branch noted Steinbach was one of three south-eastern municipalities without a greenhouse-gas baseline, urged climate adaptation and emission policies in the OCP and zoning by-law, recommended that Steinbach 'begin planning for a transit system now', asked for separated active transportation away from highways, and flagged that the regional landfill would likely reach capacity by 2036. City Planner Lacey Gaudet said a transportation plan was wanted 'within the future' but not immediately; council gave second reading without debating these points.
status_detail: No GHG inventory, climate policy, transit plan, transportation plan or landfill-siting work was brought to council in 2017–2018; the OCP passed third reading Oct 16, 2018 without public discussion of these items.
figures: Landfill serving Steinbach and 3 neighbours likely at capacity and decommissioned by end of 2036; OCP anticipates 25,000 residents in 10 years (provincial planner, 0:45:45).
reasons: one-step-at-a-time: A transportation plan is wanted in the future but 'not something we would be doing immediately'. (Lacey Gaudet (City Planner)); already-planned: Said the province's questions had been answered by staff and the plan was largely the province-approved 2015 plan. (Michael Zwaagstra)
public: Comments came from a provincial planner (Community and Regional Planning), not a resident; the speaker's name is not in the transcript.
notes: The province's GHG/transit/landfill advice was not discussed by council members in public.

title: Land sold to Centra Gas for a primary gate station for long-term gas capacity
summary: The new council sold a third-acre parcel on Hanover Road East to Centra Gas Manitoba for a primary natural gas gate station, which administration recommended 'considering the long-term planning implications', with a road widening plan for Hanover Road East.
status_detail: Sale approved Nov 20, 2018 (R18-259), subject to subdivision, variance and a road widening plan the city initiated for future planning purposes.

title: Land taken along Hanover Road East for a future road, at city cost
summary: When the city sold land to Centra Gas for a gate station, it used the sale to widen the public road allowance on a half-mile of Hanover Road East (By-law 2115) for future road building, paying the small survey and legal costs itself. Staff said it let the city consider future servicing; the mayor called it 'good planning for the future'.
status_detail: By-law 2115 passed: first and second reading Jan 15, 2019 (R19-009, R19-010), third reading Feb 5, 2019 (R19-027).
figures: City cost about $3,000 for survey and legal work (City Manager, Jan 15, 2019, 0:53:25).
mover: Jac Siemens; Damian Penner; Michael Zwaagstra
seconder: Susan Penner; Jake Hiebert; Susan Penner

title: Industrial park nearly sold out; city extends Acres Drive and buys back a lot to restock
summary: In 2019 the city sold its remaining small industrial lots (115/119 and 123 Industrial Road), and the mayor said the federally assisted Acres Drive lots were all sold. In Dec 2020 council gave first reading to a local improvement to build Acres Drive and a water main between Industrial Road and Keating Road to keep developing the industrial park, and exercised a buy-back clause to recover 88 Acres Drive, because few industrial lots were left. No industrial land strategy or supply forecast was presented.
status_detail: Lot sales (R19-023, R19-143) and the 88 Acres Drive buy-back (Dec 15, 2020) done; the Acres Drive local improvement got first reading 5-1 (R20-251), second reading in Apr 2021 and was referred to the Municipal Board (hearing Sept 9, 2021) (2021 minutes, outside this period).
figures: 115 and 119 Industrial Road $150,000 (Feb 5, 2019); 123 Industrial Road $75,000 (R19-143); 88 Acres Drive repurchased for $62,400, 80% of its 2017 sale price (Dec 15, 2020, 0:40:22); Acres Drive lots built with about $1M federal funding and sold at cost (Mayor Funk, Oct 1, 2019).
public: enVision Community Living objected to its share of the Acres Drive levy (Dec 15, 2020).
resolution_no: R19-023; R19-143; R20-251; 88 Acres Drive purchase (Dec 15, 2020)
mover: Michael Zwaagstra; Susan Penner; Michael Zwaagstra; Jac Siemens
seconder: Jac Siemens; Bill Hiebert; Susan Penner; Jake Hiebert
vote: unanimous, except R20-251 5-1 (against: Siemens; D. Penner excused)
notes: The business/economic-development side of this is covered elsewhere.

title: Supplementary water supply and second treatment plant financed: $5.375M debenture, the city's largest loan
summary: The supplementary water supply project (new supply and a second water treatment plant, started in 2018) was the largest capital project in Steinbach's history. On Feb 5, 2019 council gave third reading to By-law 2114 to borrow the full $5.375M authorized for it, over the city's usual 5-year term. Members framed it as building water capacity ahead of growth; the mayor later said federal and provincial money let the city keep supplying water 'and not having to reduce our development'.
status_detail: Debenture by-law passed unanimously (R19-030). The 2019 financial plan listed completion of the supplementary water supply system as a main 2019 project; by Feb 2020 Councillor Zwaagstra described the second plant as 'now successfully up and running'.
figures: Debt issue $5.375M with TD Bank at 3.29% (City Manager, Feb 5, 2019, 0:24:57); total project about $11M with a $5M federal grant and $600K provincial (Mayor Funk, Oct 1, 2019, 0:00:05); described as a '$12 million' plant by Councillor Zwaagstra (Feb 18, 2020, 0:22:40); debt payments of 3 mills in 2019, a one-year spike (2019 financial plan, Mar 19, 2019).
public: No member of the public spoke on the by-law.
notes: The 2018 start of the project is outside this period; total cost figures are as stated by members, not checked against a package.

title: City again objects to the RM of La Broquerie's new development plan
summary: On Mar 5, 2019 council resolved to 'further object' to the RM of La Broquerie's Development Plan By-law 06-2018, which was added to that meeting's agenda. No video transcript exists for the meeting, so the reasons are not on record; on Apr 2, 2019 Councillor Susan Penner described the La Broquerie plan as rural development 'leapfrogging' the city's boundaries instead of growing out from centres.
status_detail: Objection lodged (R19-051); the outcome of the province's review was not reported at a recorded council meeting in 2019-2020.
notes: No transcript for 2019-03-05 (video not transcribed); decision from minutes only. An earlier objection (implied by 'further object') is outside this period.

title: 2019 financial plan: $12M capital year, a 4-year capital look-ahead, and the first budget after annexation
summary: The 2019 financial plan held the mill rate at 14.09 and carried a $12M capital program led by completing the supplementary water supply. Staff gave yearly totals for the next four years only ($5.9M, $5.2M, $10.2M, $10.1M) and restated the rule of repaying all debt within five years. Councillors called it the first budget after the 2018 annexation, saying they did not yet understand its costs, and the 'planning process' that let a record project proceed without a tax increase.
status_detail: Adopted unanimously at the Mar 19, 2019 hearing (R19-063); only yearly capital totals were presented in public, with no itemized multi-year plan.
figures: Mill rate 14.09 (unchanged); capital program just under $12M; sewer rate up just over 8.5% (PUB-approved); 2020-2023 capital estimates $5.9M, $5.2M, $10.2M, $10.1M; new debt $1.5M, $2.7M repaid, year-end debt $7M; debt payments 3 mills (21% of the city rate) (all Brian Hrehirchuk, Mar 19, 2019, 0:10:37). 2018 reserve transfers included $750,000 net development-fee revenue and $675,000 for infrastructure renewal to the Capital Development Reserve (minutes R19-074).
reasons: cost: all debt on a 5-year amortization to borrow at lower rates (Brian Hrehirchuk (staff)); growth-unpredictable: first budget after annexation; council did not yet understand its costs or revenue (Jac Siemens)
public: No member of the public asked questions at the hearing (transcript).
notes: The Mar 5, 2019 meeting (no transcript) is not part of this item.

title: Stormwater handled development by development: detention ponds at Deerfield, Lexington and Harmony Lane
summary: Council funded the Deerfield detention pond and pathway in 2019 and passed plans of works for stormwater detention in Lexington Village (2019) and Harmony Lane (2020), on land dedicated by developers. Members stressed that a city this flat needs stormwater control as part of long-term planning. No city-wide stormwater or drainage master plan came before council in 2019-2020.
status_detail: Deerfield tender awarded Mar 19, 2019 (R19-064); By-law 2119 (Lexington) third reading Mar 19, 2019 (R19-072); By-law 2149 (Harmony Lane) third reading May 5, 2020 (R20-099).
figures: Deerfield detention pond and pathway tender $588,550 plus GST, from the Capital Development Reserve and gas tax reserve (City Manager, Mar 19, 2019, 0:31:57).
mover: Jac Siemens (Deerfield tender); Michael Zwaagstra (Lexington); Damian Penner, Susan Penner, Bill Hiebert (Harmony Lane)
seconder: Bill Hiebert; Damian Penner; Susan Penner; Jac Siemens; Jake Hiebert

title: City objects to an RM of Hanover plan change that would put rural residential lots on land the city needs to reach its lagoon
summary: Hanover proposed redesignating a quarter section just west of the joint boundary (west of Homestead Crescent) from agriculture to rural residential. The City Manager said this conflicted with Hanover's own plan, provincial land use policies and the Steinbach-Hanover annexation agreement. Councillors said it would block future growth to the southwest, including the only route to bring sewer service to the existing lagoon, and that Hanover had skipped the consultation the agreement requires. Council objected unanimously.
status_detail: Formal objection authorized (R19-083). The result of Hanover's hearing or any provincial decision was not reported at a recorded meeting in 2019-2020.
figures: One quarter section; the land had been in 'the long-term vision of the annexation agreement, which the province then drew back' (Councillor D. Penner, 0:21:25).
notes: Joint Action Committees: Mayor Funk re-appointed Councillor Siemens to the Steinbach-Hanover JAC and Councillor B. Hiebert to the Steinbach-La Broquerie JAC (organizational meetings Nov 5, 2019 and Nov 3, 2020; minutes). No JAC report came to a recorded meeting in 2019-2020.

title: Aquatic Centre renewal: study grant sought, ICIP application, then $1.48M renovation pulled forward to 2020
summary: In May 2019 council applied to the provincial Building Sustainable Communities program for $25,722 toward an architectural and engineering study of future repairs at the 18-year-old Aquatic Centre, and in Oct 2019 to the federal-provincial ICIP recreation stream for a $2.735M multi-year renovation. The renovation was in the long-term capital plan for 2021, but with the pool closed by COVID-19 council awarded a $1.28M tender in June 2020 and approved a $1.48M budget from the Recreation Reserve so the work would be done while capacity was limited.
status_detail: Renovation tender awarded June 2, 2020 (R20-118), funded from the city's Recreation Reserve; work was scheduled to finish so the pool could reopen about Sept 14, 2020. No ICIP grant for the pool was reported. On Oct 15, 2019 the province denied a city application to the 2019-20 Building Sustainable Communities program (minutes do not say which one).
figures: Study grant request $25,722.37 (R19-123); ICIP application: project $2,735,000, grant request $729,424.50 (Oct 1, 2019, 1:01:07; R19-197); tender $1,283,415 to Ernst Hansch Construction, total budget $1,479,415 from the Recreation Reserve Fund (R20-118; City Manager, June 2, 2020, 0:20:37).
notes: Whether the study was done with the grant (or the grant was the one denied on Oct 15, 2019) is not clear from the minutes.

title: Infill on First Street decided lot by lot; Siemens says the community plan should be revisited
summary: In July-August 2019 council split 4-3 to rezone 44 First Street (south side) for an 8-unit building (By-law 2125). Councillor Siemens, joined by both Hieberts, said the 2010 and 2014-15 community plan kept the south side single-family as a buffer and that approval would set a precedent; Councillor Zwaagstra and the majority said the plan's 'residential' designation was unchanged and medium density fit it, and a councillor said density closer to downtown reduces urban sprawl. In June 2020 Siemens supported a similar 10-unit rezoning at 78 First Street (unanimous) but said council had changed the plan 'one lot at a time' and should make re-examining First Street a priority, noting the plan is discussed every five years.
status_detail: By-law 2125 passed 4-3 (R19-152 second reading, R19-169 third reading) and By-law 2148 passed unanimously in June 2020. Siemens' call to revisit First Street in the community plan, and the five-yearly plan review he described, did not come to a recorded meeting in 2019-2020.
figures: 44 First Street: 8 units, 2 storeys, frontage variance 70 ft vs 75 ft required (V-2019-18). 78 First Street: 10 units (June 16, 2020).
reasons: already-planned: the community plan designates the area residential, so medium density needs no plan change (Michael Zwaagstra); market-decides: redeveloping old large lots is costly; single-family or side-by-side 'doesn't pay the bills' (Earl Funk)
public: Neighbours objected in July 2019, saying the south side was not part of the transitional zone. M.J. argued that a city plan, not individual variances, should guide decisions that 'affect the neighborhood for the next 50 to 100 years'.
vote: 4-3 (against: Siemens, J. Hiebert, B. Hiebert) in 2019; unanimous in 2020
notes: Similar transition-zone infill debates: Maplewood (May 2019, May 2020) and a First Street-area 8-plex in a commercial transitional POD (July 2, 2019); not itemized here.

title: Three sewer, water and road renewals from the long-term capital plan put forward for ICIP grants
summary: When the Investing in Canada Infrastructure Program opened, staff picked three projects from the city's long-term capital plan for the green infrastructure stream: Kroeker Avenue ($2.93M), Loewen Boulevard between PTH 12 and PTH 52 ($2.815M, anticipated 2021) and Brandt Street ($5.21M, anticipated 2022). Council approved all three applications and committed its share. Members said the projects were already planned and grants would help the budget.
status_detail: Applications submitted (R19-177, R19-178, R19-179). Kroeker Avenue was rebuilt in 2020 as a local improvement financed by a $1.77M debenture, and the Brandt Street renewal was brought forward for 2021 at $2.415M funded by debt and utility reserves; no ICIP grant for either was mentioned at a recorded 2019-2020 meeting.
figures: Kroeker $2,930,000 (grant request $781,431); Brandt $5,210,000; Loewen $2,815,000 with city share $750,761 (City Manager, Sept 3, 2019, 0:10:39; R19-177 to R19-179). Kroeker tender $1,797,432 (R20-052); Kroeker debenture $1.77M at 1.53% (Dec 15, 2020, 0:46:23); Brandt LIP $2.415M, $1.25M debt (Dec 15, 2020, 0:34:38).
reasons: waiting-for-funding: grants would 'very much help our budgeting' for already-planned renewals (Michael Zwaagstra)
mover: Michael Zwaagstra (Kroeker); Jake Hiebert (Brandt); Damian Penner (Loewen)
seconder: Jac Siemens; Bill Hiebert; Susan Penner
notes: ICIP outcomes for these three applications were not found in council records for 2019-2020; Loewen Boulevard's status after 2020 not checked.

title: Clearspring Greens pathway: land bought for a link, then a $625,000 resident-paid pathway approved 5-2 and later dropped
summary: Clearspring Greens, built under an old rural-standard servicing model with no sidewalks or pathways, asked for a safe walking and cycling link. In Oct 2019 the city bought 42 Carleton Drive for a possible pathway connection. In Jan 2020 council gave two readings to an 850 m lit asphalt pathway as a local improvement charged to 146 properties; Siemens and Jake Hiebert moved a cheaper limestone, unlit version, which failed 2-5. On Jan 21 council moved the lighting cost to the city's reserve. Residents cited the community plan's active transportation goals and the city-funded Deerfield path; Damian Penner said the need 'should have been planned for' when the rural zoning was approved.
status_detail: The tender was held in April 2020 because the project lacked authority to proceed; in Jan 2021 council cancelled By-law 2132 after 78 objections and denied third reading in Feb 2021 (minutes, outside this period). The Carleton Drive lot was bought (R19-194).
figures: 42 Carleton Drive purchase $115,982.50 (R19-194). Pathway 850 m, 3.0 m asphalt with lighting and fencing, $625,000, 146 benefiting properties at $4,280.82 up front or $1,044.05 a year for 5 years (minutes Jan 7, 2020, 6.2-6.3).
reasons: cost: not in favour of raising what everyone else pays for an unusually expensive sidewalk (Michael Zwaagstra); cost: proposed a cheaper limestone, unlit pathway; objected to residents paying the majority (Jac Siemens)
public: Clearspring Greens residents (e.g. S.J.) said the path was a safety need, that the city had paid for Deerfield's pathway, and that the community plan promotes active transportation networks; 78 objections were later registered.
mover: Damian Penner (LIP readings); Jac Siemens (amendment); Michael Zwaagstra (lighting)
seconder: Michael Zwaagstra; Jake Hiebert; Damian Penner
vote: 5-2 (against: Siemens, J. Hiebert); lighting change 6-1 (against: Siemens)
notes: Covered in more detail in the advocacy data (2019, 2020). The 2021 cancellation is from 2021 minutes.

title: Event centre: council commits $10M plus half a mill a year to a $42.5M downtown arena with Southeast Event Centre Inc.
summary: On Oct 1, 2019 council approved a memorandum of understanding with Southeast Event Centre Inc. (SEC), a non-profit of local business people, for a 2,500-seat downtown event centre beside the T.G. Smith Centre to replace the 1967 Centennial Arena. The city would put in $10M of capital and land and up to 0.5 mills a year toward core operating costs; SEC would raise at least $15M privately; and the city and SEC would seek $17.5M under ICIP. Members credited past councils for buying the downtown land over 20-25 years and said the project fit the 2012 decision to keep such a facility downtown.
status_detail: MOU (R19-193) and ICIP application (R19-198) approved unanimously; the 2020 financial plan included 'the start of the event centre', but no government funding decision was reported at a recorded meeting by the end of 2020, and Councillor Zwaagstra said in April 2020 that it was contingent on government and private funding.
figures: Total $42.5M ($42,491,093 in R19-198): city $10M capital, SEC at least $15M private, $17.5M requested from ICIP; city operating contribution up to 0.5 mills (about $500,000) a year (minutes R19-193; Councillor Zwaagstra, 0:33:01; Mayor Funk, 0:51:37). 2,500 seats; 500-seat hall in a second phase.
reasons: waiting-for-funding: the project requires funding from other levels of government to proceed (Earl Funk); cost: city share sized so it can be paid without extending borrowing past the 5-year maximum (Unidentified councillor)
public: G.L. presented for Southeast Event Centre Inc., asking the city to partner under the MOU. No residents spoke against at the meeting.
notes: Diarization in this file merges several councillors; only the mayor and Zwaagstra are attributed with high confidence. Funding outcome after 2020 is outside this period.

title: Council's four strategic priorities named in public, but set in closed planning sessions with no published plan
summary: The 2018-2022 council's priorities were set in its 'earliest planning sessions' and named publicly only in passing, during the Oct 2019 event centre debate: city advocacy, economic development, openness and transparency, and renewal of recreation and cultural facilities. Priority-setting and budgeting happened in the Strategic Priorities Committee and closed study sessions (e.g. July 2019, fall 2020) whose reports reached council meetings only item by item. No strategic plan document, targets or progress report was tabled at a recorded meeting in 2019-2020.
status_detail: Priorities were set and used to justify decisions (e.g. the event centre), but no written plan with goals, timelines or measures was presented publicly in this period.
notes: Strategic Priorities Committee referred to on Jan 15 and Feb 5, 2019 and May 12, 2020 (transcripts/minutes); study sessions on July 16, 2019 (opening remarks) and a fall 2020 session (minutes Sept 15, 2020). Their contents are not public in this record.

title: New residential and non-residential capital development fee by-laws adopted
summary: In November 2019 council passed By-laws 2127 (residential) and 2128 (non-residential) setting capital development fees, the charges new development pays toward growth-related city infrastructure. The meetings were not transcribed, so the fee levels and the reasons given are not on record here.
status_detail: Both by-laws passed three readings unanimously (R19-214, R19-215, R19-224 to R19-227).
figures: Fee amounts not in the minutes. For scale, 2018 net development-fee revenue of $750,000 went to the Capital Development Reserve (minutes R19-074).
mover: Michael Zwaagstra; Damian Penner; Michael Zwaagstra; Damian Penner; Jake Hiebert; Michael Zwaagstra
seconder: Damian Penner; Michael Zwaagstra; Jake Hiebert; Bill Hiebert; Michael Zwaagstra; Jac Siemens
notes: No transcripts exist for Oct 15 - Dec 17, 2019 meetings; fee levels unverified (no packages for 2019 in the project).

title: City stays in the renamed Seine Rat Roseau Watershed District
summary: Under Manitoba's new Watershed Districts Act, the Seine-Rat River Conservation District became the Seine Rat Roseau Watershed District as the province cut 18 districts to 14. Councillor Jake Hiebert, the city's board member, said Steinbach's area and funding stayed the same, and council passed By-law 2142. In Feb 2020 he asked the water co-op presenters whether their work tied in with watershed planning for drought and flooding.
figures: City funding to the district: $15,000 (Councillor J. Hiebert, Jan 21, 2020, 0:22:17).

title: New Steinbach Emergency Plan by-law and a mutual-aid agreement with the RM of Hanover
summary: Council adopted By-law 2134, the Steinbach Emergency Plan, in Nov-Dec 2019 and a memorandum of understanding with the RM of Hanover for mutual aid, including evacuation, in emergencies. Amendments to the plan were approved in Dec 2020. These were the period's only resilience measures; no climate plan or climate risk discussion came to council (a 2019 Climate Change Conference invitation was simply received as information, Aug 20, 2019).
status_detail: By-law 2134 passed (first reading Nov 19, R19-253, R19-254); Hanover MOU approved (R19-255); 2020 amendments approved Dec 15, 2020 (R20-259).
mover: Michael Zwaagstra; Jac Siemens; Damian Penner; Michael Zwaagstra
seconder: Damian Penner; Jake Hiebert; Michael Zwaagstra; Jac Siemens
notes: Minutes only (no transcripts for Nov-Dec 2019).

title: Millbrook Market secondary plan adopted for 20 acres on PTH 12 North; an old Parkhill secondary plan repealed
summary: A developer's secondary plan (By-law 2136) for about 20 acres at 110 PTH 12 North set out a mixed-use 'Millbrook Market' of commercial, high-density residential and park space; the land had been held as Development Reserve under the community plan's commercial designation. Council passed it with the matching CMX rezoning in March 2020. At the same meeting council repealed the older Parkhill secondary plan (By-law 2072) at the developer's request because, staff said, it added nothing to the approved concept plan and zoning.
status_detail: By-law 2136 given third reading Mar 3, 2020 (R20-043) with rezoning By-law 2137; repeal By-law 2143 passed the same night (R20-047). Secondary plans in this period were developer-led, site by site.
figures: About 20 acres; CMX zoning allows residential buildings up to 8 storeys (May 5, 2020 transcript).
public: No one objected at the Mar 3, 2020 hearing (minutes 6.8). The developers (named in minutes) presented the plan.

title: Council celebrates a decade of growth but presents no population projection
summary: Councillor Susan Penner opened a Jan 2020 meeting with a decade review: $721M in building permits and 1,859 dwelling units from 2009 to 2019, about $115M invested in infrastructure, and 87% population growth from 1996 to 2016, concluding the economy 'shows no signs of slowing down'. The mayor reported building permits monthly (e.g. 257 units and $58.5M in 2020 by mid-December). No population projection, growth study or estimate of future servicing needs was presented in 2019-2020.
status_detail: Growth was tracked backward (permits, census) but no forward projection was tabled at a recorded meeting in this period.
figures: Permits 2009-2019 $720,997,744.60 (45% residential); 1,859 dwelling units; infrastructure 2009-2018 $100.7M (about $115M with the water plant); population +87% 1996-2016 (Councillor S. Penner, Jan 21, 2020, 0:00:17). 2020: 257 units and just over $58.5M in permits to mid-December (Mayor Funk, Dec 15, 2020, 0:42:29).

title: Regional water co-op proposal heard and received as information; councillor asks why Steinbach would give up control
summary: On Feb 18, 2020 Landmark Planning & Design and a Friesen Drillers hydrogeologist, working for the Manitoba Water Services Board, presented the idea of an East Region Water Co-op for southeast municipalities, for redundancy and long-term supply. They warned that Steinbach draws from one aquifer with competing users nearby. A councillor (most likely Zwaagstra) asked why the city would join, given 'abundant' water and its new second treatment plant; the presenters said membership could be partial and the city might never need it. Council took it as information and took no further step.
status_detail: Received as information (minutes items 9.1-9.4). No follow-up, staff report or decision on joining was found in 2019-2020; the existing 2022-2026 report notes council revisited a regional water co-op in January 2022.
figures: Steinbach's second water treatment plant: '$12 million' (councillor, 0:22:40). Pembina Valley Water Co-op cited as a model (14 municipalities).
reasons: already-planned: abundant water supply, a new $12M treatment plant and full local control (Michael Zwaagstra (medium-confidence attribution)); local-control: 'why would we consider giving that up' (Michael Zwaagstra (medium-confidence attribution))
public: Delegation (initials only): D.T. of Landmark Planning & Design said planners should think '30, 40, 50, 80 years away' and that water supplies aren't guaranteed; J.B., a hydrogeologist, said Steinbach has no redundancy if it lost a well field and faces competing use in its drawdown area.
notes: Which councillor asked the 0:22:40 question is not certain (Zwaagstra most likely).

title: Annual traffic counts used to press the province on PTH 12 and Loewen Boulevard
summary: The city's yearly WSP traffic count (21 intersections) showed PTH 12 peak-hour traffic growing 1.2-3.6% a year over 10 years and sharp jumps on PTH 52. Council forwarded the report to Manitoba Infrastructure and repeated its request that the PTH 12/Loewen Boulevard intersection be made a priority. Members said the counts give evidence for requests to the province; the city did not have its own transportation master plan.
status_detail: Report forwarded with the request (R20-034); no provincial commitment was reported in 2020.
figures: PTH 12 p.m. peak volumes +1.2% to 3.6% a year over 10 years; PTH 52 eastbound/westbound through movements up 28-43% at PTH 12 and 20-31% at Industrial Road over 2018 (minutes 10.1); close to 3,000 vehicles an hour at peak through Loewen/PTH 12 (Mayor Funk, 0:47:21).
reasons: provincial-responsibility: PTH 12 upgrades are the province's; the city supplies evidence (Michael Zwaagstra)
notes: A separate report covers traffic congestion in detail.

title: Councillors flag north-end road capacity (Bush Farm, Keating, Park Road West); mayor says a plan is needed
summary: Approving the next phase of the Parkhill subdivision in March 2020, Councillor Susan Penner asked that traffic on the north-end roads be put on the July study session agenda as density grows, and Councillor Damian Penner said the whole north end (Bush Farm, Keating, Park Road West) should be looked at together. The mayor agreed it needed more than one study session and that council should 'come up with a plan' for the roads because the city is growing.
status_detail: No north-end road or transportation plan came back to a recorded council meeting in 2020; study session contents are not public.
reasons: study-first: refer to the July study session (Susan Penner)
public: A resident (named in minutes) objected to added traffic on Bush Farm Road.

title: 2020 financial plan: capital look-ahead jumps to $24.8M and $31.5M as the event centre is booked, amid COVID uncertainty
summary: Presented Apr 7, 2020, early in the pandemic, the 2020 plan cut the mill rate 2.8% to 13.7 (a reassessment year), raised the wastewater rate 9.5% under an earlier PUB approval, and carried a $13.1M capital program including the start of the event centre. The four-year look-ahead rose sharply ($24.8M in 2021, then $31.5M, $14.4M, $14.6M) because of the event centre. Councillor Zwaagstra said big items such as the event centre were contingent on government and private funding and some spending could be delayed.
status_detail: Adopted unanimously (R20-074). Staff warned some items might be deferred because of COVID-19; again only yearly totals of the multi-year capital program were given in public.
figures: Mill rate 13.7 (-2.8%); wastewater rate +9.5% (PUB-approved), water unchanged; capital program $13.1M; revenues just under $31M; 2021-2024 capital estimates $24.8M, $31.5M, $14.4M, $14.6M; debt payments 2.1 mills (15.5% of the city rate) (Brian Hrehirchuk, Apr 7, 2020, 0:21:12); year-end debt $7.8M (Mayor Funk, 0:39:15).
reasons: waiting-for-funding: event centre contingent on government and private funding (Michael Zwaagstra); growth-unpredictable: pandemic uncertainty; some items may be delayed until there is more clarity (Brian Hrehirchuk (staff))
public: No member of the public spoke at the hearing (transcript).

title: City objects to provincial Bill 48: developer appeals and new regional planning boards
summary: Bill 48 (2020) proposed letting applicants appeal council land-use decisions and conditions to the Municipal Board, and created a Capital Planning Region around Winnipeg with power to set up other planning regions later. The City Manager said it threatened 'local autonomy in planning' and could add a regional layer of process, though the capital region would not include Steinbach. Councillors said Steinbach's planning works well, that Municipal Board rulings (including on annexation) had overridden the city before, and that appeals would add delay. Council authorized staff to send its concerns to the province.
status_detail: Concerns forwarded to Manitoba Municipal Relations (R20-120). No further council discussion of the bill or a regional planning board for the southeast in 2020.
reasons: local-control: the city is good at land planning; a regional or appeal layer adds red tape and removes the final say (Jac Siemens); local-control: potential loss of local autonomy; possible new regional boards adding process (Troy Warkentin (staff))
notes: The bill's later history (reintroduced as Bill 37 in 2021) is outside this period and not taken from council records.

title: Clearspring Greens pathway built; wider active transportation network left to the future
summary: After residents objected to the first plan, council cancelled it and approved a cheaper asphalt pathway with costs split 50/50 and capped at $1,610 per lot, the same as the sidewalk capital development fee. The path was built in 2021. Councillor Siemens said it would likely become part of a wider path around that end of the city 'within the next decade'. No active transportation plan was discussed in 2021–2022.
status_detail: Original plan cancelled (R21-011, 78 objections) and new plan approved (R21-012); path completed by December 2021 with borrowing reduced to about $137,000 after 60 prepayments. Per the 2022–2026 record, an Active Transportation Plan was accepted only in May 2025 (R25-096).
figures: Resident cap $1,610 per parcel; debt authorized ~$233,000, borrowed ~$137,000 over 5 years at 2.42% (City Manager, Dec 21, 2021, 0:32:12).
public: 78 objections were registered to the first local improvement plan (minutes R21-011).

title: City applies for federal asset-management grant as it starts a formal asset management system
summary: Council voted to apply to the Federation of Canadian Municipalities' Municipal Asset Management Program for $50,000 toward asset management software, an asset management policy and strategy, and a condition assessment of all hard-surfaced roads.
