The city manager said Steinbach was moving into the 'active phase' of a formal asset management system, following a provincial push. There was little debate.
status_detail: The application was approved unanimously (R21-020). No report on the grant result, the software or the road condition assessment came to a recorded meeting in 2021–2022. Per the existing 2022–2026 report, the asset management policy, strategy and plan were adopted only in October 2023.
figures: Grant sought $50,000; city share $20,000 from the 2021 operating budget; total $70,000 (City Manager, transcript 0:14:14; minutes R21-020).
notes: Whether the FCM grant was awarded was not found in the 2021–2022 records.

title: City completes decades-long downtown land assembly for the Event Centre
summary: Council bought 340 Hanover Street, 310 Hanover Street and five lots on Reimer Avenue next to the existing rinks 'for future municipal purposes'. Staff and councillors described these as the last pieces of a long-term strategy, begun by earlier councils over 25 years ago, to assemble downtown land for a recreation facility, now the Southeast Event Centre and its parking.
status_detail: All three purchases approved unanimously (R21-015, R21-097, R22-103). The Reimer Avenue land was paid for from the Recreation Reserve Fund.
figures: 340 Hanover St $250,000 (R21-015); 310 Hanover St $475,000 (R21-097); 305–329 Reimer Ave $1,400,000 from Steinbach Credit Union (R22-103), from the Recreation Reserve Fund (Zwaagstra, Apr 19, 2022, 0:22:09).
seconder: Jac Siemens (R21-015); Damian Penner (R21-097); Susan Penner (R22-103)

title: Council objects again to provincial Bill 37 and the prospect of forced planning regions
summary: Bill 37 (The Planning Amendment and City of Winnipeg Charter Amendment Act) would create the Capital Planning Region and let the province set up other planning regions by regulation, possibly including Steinbach, and widen appeals of council land-use conditions to the Municipal Board. Council told the city manager to send the province the same concerns it had sent about the earlier Bill 48 in June 2020. Councillors objected to loss of local decision-making, delays, and planning districts in which each municipality gets a vote.
status_detail: Letter of concern authorized unanimously (R21-025). No provincial response was reported at a recorded meeting in 2021–2022.
reasons: neighbours-disagree: regional planning districts where each municipality gets a vote 'can cause some real tensions'; worried a district could be forced even after consultation (Michael Zwaagstra); local-autonomy: more Municipal Board appeals take decisions from elected council to non-elected people and delay development (Michael Zwaagstra); local-autonomy: Steinbach would lose autonomy over how it builds the city; cited the Municipal Board's handling of the annexation (Jac Siemens)
notes: Whether Bill 37 passed in this form, and whether any planning region now includes Steinbach, was not checked against provincial records.

title: City sells industrial lots and opens new ones on Acres Drive as supply runs short
summary: Through 2021–2022 council sold city-owned industrial land (20 acres on Tower Avenue; a lot on Acres Drive bought back from an owner who had not built), approved subdivisions of industrial lots, extended Acres Drive to Keating Road as a local improvement, and approved new 1.5–2-acre lots created by the Steinbach Community Development Corporation. Councillors repeatedly said industrial lots were 'desperately getting into short supply' and in high demand.
status_detail: Tower Avenue ($645,900) and 88 Acres Drive ($124,900) sales approved Feb 2, 2021; Acres Drive extension By-law 2161 given third reading Feb 15, 2022 after Municipal Board approval (R22-044); three ~2-acre lots approved Oct 4, 2022 (R22-223) and four 1.5-acre lots Dec 6, 2022; the $3.1M borrowing for Acres Drive was cancelled (By-law 2219, first reading Dec 6, 2022) because the Community Development Corporation could pay.
figures: 45 Tower Ave 20 acres sold for $645,900 (minutes Feb 2, 2021); 88 Acres Dr $124,900 (R21-024); Acres Drive local improvement borrowing up to $3.1M (Zwaagstra, Feb 15, 2022, 0:33:08), later cancelled (City Manager, Dec 6, 2022, 0:18:12).
reasons: market-decides: industrial subdivisions are 'market-driven' and meet a need (Mar 16, 2021, moving subdivision R21-058) (Jake Hiebert)
mover: Susan Penner (R21-024); Michael Zwaagstra (R22-044); Damian Penner (R22-223)
seconder: Michael Zwaagstra (R21-024); Susan Penner (R22-044); Jake Hiebert (R22-223)
notes: No minutes were found for Dec 6, 2022; those decisions are from the transcript ('That is carried'). No overall industrial land supply study or target was presented in 2021–2022.

title: Five-year economic development office with the Chamber, under council's 'economic development' strategic priority
summary: Council adopted terms of reference to fund an economic development office run by the Steinbach Chamber of Commerce, matching private funding up to $65,000 a year for five years (2021–2025). Councillor Damian Penner tied it to economic development being one of council's four strategic priorities; the mayor called it 'post-COVID planning'. In October 2022 the Chamber reported setting up a separate Steinbach Economic Development Corporation and an investment-attraction and workforce study.
status_detail: Terms of reference adopted unanimously (R21-049). The Chamber gave council a progress presentation on Oct 18, 2022.
figures: City grant matching private funding to a maximum of $65,000 a year, 2021–2025 inclusive (minutes Mar 2, 2021).
public: The Chamber chair (C.B.) told council in Oct 2022 that the city's Community Development Corporation is 'about land use planning, managing the city's land assets that are acquired for future industrial and infrastructure needs', separate from the new economic development corporation.
notes: The four 2018–2022 strategic priorities were listed by a councillor on Oct 1, 2019 (outside this period) as city advocacy, economic development, openness and transparency, and recreation and cultural facility renewal; no strategic plan document was tabled in 2021–2022.

title: Traffic handled through annual counts and provincial partnerships, without a transportation master plan
summary: Each year council received the WSP traffic count program for about 24 intersections and forwarded it to Manitoba Infrastructure with priority requests (Loewen Boulevard/PTH 12 in 2021; signals at PTH 52 West and Giesbrecht Street in 2022). Council approved the $8.275M Loewen Boulevard/PTH 12 intersection renewal, cost-shared with the province. Councillors said traffic was discussed at long-term planning sessions, but in September 2022 Councillor Siemens said there was no definitive plan for the city's north-east traffic.
status_detail: Traffic reports accepted and forwarded (R21-046; R22-038); intersection local improvement By-law 2187 given first and second readings Dec 7, 2021 (R21-250, R21-251). No transportation master plan was commissioned in 2021–2022.
figures: Loewen/PTH 12 renewal $8.275M: borrowing $3.5M over 5 years, grants and other funding $4.545M, reserves $230,000 (City Manager, Dec 7, 2021, 0:19:21). 2021 counts at 24 intersections, weekday 3–6 p.m. (minutes Feb 15, 2022).
reasons: provincial-responsibility: highway intersections depend on Manitoba Infrastructure; the city sends its priorities each year (Michael Zwaagstra); one-step-at-a-time: road work follows development (Sep 6, 2022) (Earl Funk)
public: K.P., for a landowner at the Loewen/PTH 12 corner, asked for a third westbound lane and a median opening (Dec 7, 2021); the mayor said the hearing was only about the borrowing.
mover: M. Zwaagstra (R21-046, R21-251, R22-038); J. Siemens (R21-250)
seconder: J. Hiebert (R21-046); D. Penner (R21-250, R22-038); B. Hiebert (R21-251)

title: Priorities and long-term planning handled in closed committee and study sessions
summary: Council's strategic planning in 2021–2022 happened in its Strategic Priorities Committee and twice-yearly study sessions (usually July and November), which are not recorded. Staff referred to by-laws first discussed there; Councillor Siemens said long-term issues such as traffic had been discussed at these sessions 'for over 5 years'; Councillor Jake Hiebert told residents the new council would spend a day and a half setting spending priorities in November 2022. No strategic plan, goals or progress report was tabled at a recorded meeting.
status_detail: No strategic plan document was published in this period. Per the 2022–2026 record, the 2022–26 priorities were four headings set in unrecorded sessions.
reasons: already-planned: long-term issues are discussed twice a year at planning sessions (Jac Siemens)
notes: The 2018–2022 four strategic priorities were named on Oct 1, 2019 (outside this period): city advocacy, economic development, openness and transparency, and recreation and cultural facility renewal.

title: Annual financial plans fund growth projects within a five-year debt rule
summary: Council adopted the 2021 plan (mill rate unchanged at 13.7, capital program $19.6M including the start of the Event Centre and Brandt Street utility renewal) and the 2022 plan (14.1 mills, $25.3M new capital and $13.9M renewal). The Municipal Act requires a five-year capital expenditure program, but only annual totals were presented. Councillors defended the long-standing rule of borrowing only on five-year terms, which forces choices about what gets built; reserves rose to $34.1M by end of 2021 for 'larger projects that are on the horizon in our long-term capital plan'.
status_detail: Both plans adopted unanimously (R21-064, R22-076). The five-year capital program itself was not presented or discussed at a recorded meeting.
figures: 2021: capital $19.6M, revenue ~$32M, 13.7 mills (Hrehirchuk, Apr 6, 2021, 0:19:59). 2022: 14.1 mills, $25.3M new capital, $13.9M renewal (minutes Apr 5, 2022). Reserves $34.1M and debt $6.1M at Dec 31, 2021 (Thiessen, Jun 7, 2022, 0:21:33).
reasons: cost: five-year debt 'does force us to make some choices as far as what we're going to build', but everything is paid off quickly (Michael Zwaagstra); growth-pays: fast growth 'comes with a lot of problems' but lets the city hold taxes down (Jac Siemens)
public: No one spoke at the 2022 budget hearing (minutes Apr 5, 2022).
notes: The April 5, 2022 budget hearing video has no audio; 2022 figures are from the minutes.

title: Council celebrates record growth but adopts no population projection
summary: Monthly and year-end building permit reports were the main way council discussed growth. 2021 was the third-best year on record with about $101M in permits; councillors said growth 'shows no signs of slowing down'. The mayor relayed the new economic development officer's estimate that Steinbach could be Manitoba's second-largest city by 2051, and said the city had 'never, ever, ever had negative growth'. No population projection was tabled or used in a decision in 2021–2022.
status_detail: No official population projection was adopted. The 2022–2026 record shows the first projection (34,085 by 2041) came with the 2025 OCP.
figures: 2021 building permits about $101M, third-highest year (Zwaagstra and S. Penner, Jan 18, 2022, 0:05:18–0:06:10); 2020 permits ~$66M (Hrehirchuk, Apr 6, 2021).
reasons: growth-unpredictable: 'The life cycle of a city, of Steinbach, is not easy to predict' (Nov 1, 2022) (Jac Siemens)
notes: The 2051 'second-largest city' estimate is attributed to the economic development officer and was not verified.

title: Council debates keeping industrial parks industrial: school rezoning refused, retail allowed case by case
summary: Council refused to rezone a church site in an industrial park for a school (May 2021), arguing a rezoning is permanent and would saddle future councils with sidewalks and traffic issues. It then split on retail in light-industrial units: a retail store was allowed by conditional use in April 2022 (5-2), a request for retail on a whole site was refused in October 2022, and a limited retail use for a charity's book sales was allowed in November 2022 (5-2). Several councillors said industrial parks are subsidized to attract industry; Councillor Jake Hiebert asked council to decide what the area should be instead of ruling case by case.
status_detail: Industrial zoning was kept (By-law 2170 denied R21-091; CU-2022-02 denied R22-224), but two retail conditional uses were approved on split votes (R22-077, R22-262). No review of the industrial zoning or of retail in M1 zones followed in 2022.
reasons: protect-land-use: a rezoning stays 'forever'; industrial parks are subsidized to attract industry, so retail belongs in commercial areas (Michael Zwaagstra); protect-land-use: rezoning passes problems such as walkways to future councils (Damian Penner); protect-land-use: subsidized industrial space undercuts developers of commercial retail space (Oct 2022) (Susan Penner)
public: Applicants (a church school; S.H., owner of a multi-unit industrial site; ROC Eastman, a children's recreation charity) asked for the uses; no residents objected.
mover: S. Penner (R21-090); D. Penner (R21-091); J. Siemens (R22-077); M. Zwaagstra (R22-224, R22-262)
seconder: J. Siemens (R21-090); J. Hiebert (R21-091); B. Hiebert (R22-077); J. Siemens (R22-224, R22-262)
vote: R21-090 defeated 2-5; R21-091 5-2 (against: S. Penner, J. Siemens); R22-077 5-2 (against: M. Zwaagstra, J. Hiebert); R22-224 unanimous; R22-262 5-2 (against: D. Penner, J. Hiebert)
notes: The April 5, 2022 meeting (CU-2022-01) has no audio; reasons for that split vote are not recorded beyond the minutes' note of questions on employees and parking.

title: Official Community Plan changed site by site; no full review begun
summary: Council amended the Official Community Plan for individual developments: Park Road West west of Clearspring Mall (By-law 2177/2183, residential to commercial, 2021), Old Tom Road and Loewen Boulevard (By-law 2211, 2022; see separate item) and 6 First Street (By-law 2216, industrial to central business district, 2022). Councillor Zwaagstra described the OCP as a document 'we revise every 5 years'; Councillor Damian Penner said the city was 'booming' and the OCP 'does need to be looked at' to open land for growth. No comprehensive OCP review was started at a recorded meeting in 2021–2022. Councillor Siemens opposed the First Street change as outside his long-term vision for the CBD.
status_detail: By-law 2183 adopted (third reading R21-234, Nov 2, 2021); By-law 2216 given first (R22-229, 6-1) and second (R22-251, 5-2) readings and third reading on Jul 4, 2023 (R23-141, against Siemens). A new OCP (By-law 2244) was adopted only in September 2025.
figures: Park Road West development about 67–68 acres, 139 residential lots (Zwaagstra, Jun 15 and Aug 17, 2021; Jake Hiebert, Aug 17, 2021).
reasons: market-decides: the Park Road West mix is 'obviously what the market in Steinbach is driving at this time' (seconder of R21-173, addressed as 'Councillor Huber') (Jake Hiebert)
public: Residents near 6 First Street raised concerns about setbacks and the building (Nov 1, 2022); no objections were filed on the 2021 Park Road West amendment.
seconder: B. Hiebert (R21-136, R21-234); M. Zwaagstra (R21-157); J. Hiebert (R21-173); S. Penner (R22-229); D. Penner (R22-251)
vote: 2021 amendments unanimous; R22-229 6-1 (against: J. Siemens); R22-251 5-2 (against: J. Siemens, J. Hiebert)
notes: The date of the previous comprehensive OCP review was not confirmed from council records in this period.

title: Council declines to commit to an East Region Water Co-op; engineers' supply report promised but not seen
summary: Landmark Planning & Design briefed council on the RM of Ritchot's search for a new well (June 2021) and, in January 2022, on a proposed East Region Water Co-op modelled on the Pembina Valley Water Co-op, asking whether Steinbach was interested. Councillors said Steinbach's supply and its new water treatment plant were adequate and asked what the compelling reason to join would be; the delegate replied it depended on whether the city's water forecasts looked 30–40 years ahead. The mayor referred the question to administration for an engineers' report on current supply.
status_detail: Received as information; no report on long-term water supply came back to a recorded meeting in 2022, and the delegation did not return in 2022. The water treatment plant's final change orders ($726,798.90) were approved July 6, 2021 (R21-143; no transcript for that meeting).
figures: Five wells drawing from the limestone aquifer, over 3,000 gallons per minute (Bill Hiebert, Aug 17, 2021, 0:00:15). Secondary water treatment plant cost about $11M (Zwaagstra, Nov 1, 2022, 1:33:31). WTP change orders $726,798.90 (R21-143).
reasons: already-planned: Steinbach has adequate supply and a new treatment plant 'good for the long term'; questioned spending tax dollars on a co-op (Michael Zwaagstra); study-first: 'we have to get the numbers and the facts' before committing; plant built to grow with the city (Earl Funk)
public: D.T. of Landmark Planning & Design (delegation, Jun 15, 2021 and Jan 4, 2022) said other municipalities plan water supply 20–30 years ahead and that a tested alternate source would give redundancy, as Winkler has by buying a third of its water from the Pembina Valley Water Co-op.
vote: consensus (received as information; referred to administration)
notes: Whether administration prepared the engineers' report internally is unknown; it was not tabled at a recorded meeting in 2022.

title: Steinbach joins seven-municipality review of silica sand mining to protect the shared aquifer
summary: Council agreed to join a regional group of southeastern municipalities and share the cost of an independent review of the proposed silica sand mine near Vivian, including its possible effects on the aquifer and on municipal infrastructure. The mayor and city manager were appointed to the regional committee.
status_detail: Approved unanimously (R21-194). The review's findings were not reported at a recorded council meeting in 2021–2022.
figures: Cost-sharing among member municipalities; amount not stated (minutes R21-194).

title: Southeast Event Centre: design, five-year financing and a $61M construction contract
summary: Council hired Verne Reimer Architecture for design (Sep 2021), passed the local improvement plan to borrow $7.5M over five years toward an estimated $42.5M facility (Dec 2021–Apr 2022), and in November 2022 awarded a reduced-scope construction contract of $61M after tenders came in near $75–80M. Councillors called it a 60-year, generational facility for a growing city and the largest project in the city's history. The Southeast Events Group raised its pledge from $15M to $25.5M; the city's share rose to about a third.
status_detail: Design contract R21-199; By-law 2186 readings R21-204, R21-249, R22-100; construction contract R22-254 (Nov 1, 2022). Centennial Arena to be demolished in summer 2023. Further borrowing was flagged as possible if additional federal/provincial grants did not come.
figures: Design $1,898,430 (R21-199). Dec 2021: total $42.5M, city $10M, private $15M, federal/provincial $17.5M, borrowing $7.5M over 5 years (Zwaagstra, Dec 7, 2021, 0:08:58). Nov 2022: lowest bid ~$75.3M, reduced GMP $61M, ~$66M with land; Southeast Events Group $25.5M; city about 35% (Zwaagstra, 1:33:31), about $21M (Siemens, 1:36:55) or $23M (S. Penner, 1:46:17).
reasons: now-or-never: if not now, 'it will be another 20 years' before a facility of this size; private and government money would be lost (Jac Siemens); cost: higher costs draw on reserves and the operating fund and 'will have an impact in our future finances' (Michael Zwaagstra)
public: Letters to the Dec 7, 2021 hearing questioned the scope and 2,500 seats (per Zwaagstra); no one spoke at the hearing.
mover: M. Zwaagstra (R21-199, R22-100, R22-254); S. Penner (R21-204); J. Siemens (R21-249)
seconder: J. Siemens (R21-199, R22-254); D. Penner (R21-204); M. Zwaagstra (R21-249); S. Penner (R22-100)
notes: The Event Centre is covered in more depth by the taxes-and-spending report.

title: Talk of a 'more regional approach': joint committees, a regional library idea and an AMM nomination
summary: The mayor kept councillors on joint action committees with the RM of Hanover (Jac Siemens) and the RM of La Broquerie (Bill Hiebert); their work was not reported publicly. In May 2022 Councillor Susan Penner asked why the Jake Epp Library could not become a regional library; Councillor Damian Penner said there was 'a numbers case' since one in six patrons live outside the city, but left it to neighbouring residents to press their councils. In November 2022 council endorsed Councillor Siemens for the AMM executive, with Councillor Penner saying council wanted 'a more regional approach with certain projects'.
status_detail: Appointments ratified (R21-227); library question received as information; AMM endorsement carried Nov 1, 2022. No joint plan or regional service agreement came forward in 2021–2022; per the 2022–2026 record, regional library talks ended in January 2026.
figures: About 1 in 6 library patrons are non-residents; non-resident membership about $110 (Damian Penner, May 3, 2022, 0:19:01–0:21:35).
reasons: neighbours-decide: regionalizing the library depends on residents of other municipalities asking their councils (Damian Penner)

title: Council refuses to split a rural lot in development reserve land to protect orderly future growth
summary: Council denied a request to subdivide a 6.75-acre unserviced property on Hespeler Street South into a 2-acre home lot and a remainder. Administration and councillors cited the Development Reserve 1 policy, which keeps land in large holdings so the city can extend sewer and water in sequence without 'leapfrogging'. Councillors acknowledged landowners' frustration but said council must look 20–30 years ahead.
status_detail: Denied unanimously (R21-238).
figures: Parcel about 6.75 acres; proposed lots 2 acres and 4.75 acres; DR-1 minimum 20 acres (City Manager and Siemens, 0:19:03–0:20:32).
reasons: orderly-growth: development must be incremental and serviced; no leapfrogging, private wells or septic fields inside the city (Jac Siemens); cost: 2-acre lots make it 'very expensive to bring services across' to future developments (Damian Penner)
public: The applicant acted for the owners (initials only); they were not quoted. Councillors noted that owners of large rural-style lots in DR-1 land are frustrated at waiting for development.

title: Room to grow for city services: operations yard land and a new landfill cell
summary: Council closed an unused road allowance so it could be consolidated with land the city expects to use to expand the operations yard over several years (Feb 2022), and awarded a $1.81M expansion of the landfill's active cell, paid from the environmental reserve, because the current cell was expected to reach capacity at the end of 2023 (Aug 2022). The mayor said facilities must grow as the city grows.
status_detail: By-law 2199 second and third readings (R22-036, R22-037); landfill cell tender awarded (R22-194). No long-range plan for public works or the landfill's overall life was presented.
figures: Landfill active cell expansion $1,809,945.52 plus taxes, sole bidder EarthMax Construction (R22-194), from the environmental reserve (Siemens, 0:14:28).
seconder: D. Penner (R22-036); M. Zwaagstra (R22-037); B. Hiebert (R22-194)

title: Making room for partners' long-term growth: a second gas supply and Bethesda hospital expansion
summary: Council granted a variance so Centra Gas could build a pressure-regulating station for a secondary gas supply, which Centra said was needed for 20-year forecast growth in Steinbach and area (Mar 2022). It also rezoned three Hospital Street lots for the long-planned northward expansion of Bethesda Regional Health Centre (Aug–Sep 2022).
status_detail: Variance V-2022-01 approved (R22-051); By-law 2214 first reading R22-186, second and third readings R22-206/R22-207, all unanimous.
figures: Centra station site 0.72 acres in DR-1 land where 20 acres is the minimum (City Manager, Mar 1, 2022, 0:09:26).
public: Centra Gas wrote that the station would provide 'for a 20-year forecasted growth in Steinbach and area' (minutes Mar 1, 2022). R.P., for Southern Health–Santé Sud, said the hospital had a long-term plan to move toward Loewen Boulevard.
mover: J. Hiebert (R22-051); M. Zwaagstra (R22-186); J. Siemens (R22-206, R22-207)
seconder: M. Zwaagstra (R22-051); S. Penner (R22-186); J. Hiebert (R22-206, R22-207)

title: Large Loewen Boulevard–Old Tom Road development approved over residents' calls for long-term planning
summary: Council amended the OCP (By-law 2211) and rezoned land annexed in 2018 at Loewen Boulevard and Old Tom Road for a multi-phase residential and commercial development, and approved its first 95-lot subdivision. Neighbours raised flooding, a creek buffer, traffic, active transportation and crowded schools, and one asked council to 'do some serious long-term planning'. Councillors relied on engineering reports and on the market; the mayor said road improvements follow development; Councillor Siemens said traffic was part of council's long-term planning sessions but 'there's not a definitive plan'.
status_detail: OCP By-law 2211 second reading (R22-201) and rezonings and subdivision approved Sep 6, 2022 (R22-202, R22-203, R22-205); By-law 2213's second reading was rescinded Oct 4, 2022 because of a notice error and re-given Nov 1, 2022 (R22-250). By-law 2211 got third reading Jun 6, 2023 (R23-115).
figures: First subdivision: 95 parcels including 30 single-family and 60 low-density lots (City Manager, 1:23:35). Lift station $1.2–1.4M (developer, 1:05:38).
reasons: one-step-at-a-time: 'as development comes, we let the development happen and then we can work on the road system' (Earl Funk); market-decides: housing mix follows supply and demand; phasing must make sense for the developer (Susan Penner); already-planned: traffic is discussed at twice-yearly long-term planning sessions, though no definitive plan exists (Jac Siemens); growth-is-goal: approvals are about letting people live and do business in Steinbach, not tax revenue; 'It's why we annex land' (Michael Zwaagstra)
public: R.F. (neighbour) opposed the bylaws over flooding, a missing creek buffer, traffic and school capacity, and asked for a traffic impact study, an active transportation plan, a runoff plan and a review of the OCP. J.C. supported the development but asked about intersections, dust, speed and paving. D.E. asked for a traffic count when the road is open. G.P., an adjacent farmer, asked for uniform fencing to keep debris off farmland. Their claims about drainage were disputed by the developer's engineering report and are unproven.
mover: M. Zwaagstra (R22-201); J. Siemens (R22-202); S. Penner (R22-203); D. Penner (R22-205)
seconder: S. Penner (R22-201); D. Penner (R22-202); M. Zwaagstra (R22-203); J. Siemens (R22-205)
notes: School capacity was raised by a resident; council did not respond on it at the meeting.

title: Mayor opens the new term calling for a 20–30-year plan
summary: At the first regular meeting after the 2022 election (all incumbents returned), Mayor Funk said the last term had finished its project list and the new term should 'take our sights off of a 4-year plan' and plan 20–30 years ahead, with capital plans, projects and infrastructure renewal, because Steinbach will keep growing through immigration and business.
status_detail: No 20–30-year plan was tabled in 2022. The 2022–2026 record shows the call did not produce a strategic plan, though a new OCP (2025) followed.

title: Lift Station 2 upgrade and Loewen force main to open east-side subdivisions
summary: Council approved, borrowed for and built an upgrade of Lift Station 2 on Loewen Boulevard with a new force main, because east-side subdivisions could not proceed without more sewer capacity. When tenders came in high in 2023 the force main part was pushed to 2024, then awarded with a reduced scope.
status_detail: Local improvement by-law 2221 (third reading Mar 21, 2023), tender awarded Oct 17, 2023, $2M debenture from TD (By-law 2239, third reading Mar 5, 2024), Loewen force main awarded Mar 19, 2024. Work was under way in 2024.
figures: Estimate $2.265M with $2M borrowed over 5 years (Warkentin, transcript 2023-01-03 0:11:29); tender $1,996,642.57 plus $250,000 from the utility reserve (minutes R23-213); TD rate 5.41% (transcript 2023-12-19 0:51:25); force main sole bid $570,310, awarded at $491,693 after reducing scope (transcript 2024-03-19 2:19:08; minutes R24-065)
reasons: cost: force main portion postponed to 2024 to keep the 2023 tender within budget (Michael Zwaagstra)
public: No objections at the Jan 3, 2023 public hearing.
mover: Jac Siemens (R23-008); Michael Zwaagstra (R23-054, R23-213, R24-065)
seconder: Michael Zwaagstra (R23-008); Damian Penner (R23-054); Jac Siemens (R23-213, R24-065)

title: Southeast Event Centre cost rises to $69.2M; council funds the gap
summary: The event centre, approved in November 2022 as a generational project, rose from $61M to $69.153M after soil and mechanical redesign issues. Council added $5M of contingency borrowing in 2023 and in December approved an $8.153M change order funded from operating funds, a provincial grant, reserves and new debt. Members said waiting would only have cost more.
status_detail: Change order and funding approved unanimously Dec 19, 2023; construction continued through 2024. The operating agreement was pulled from the Dec 2024 agendas.
figures: Total $69.153M (Zwaagstra, transcript 0:32:15); extra $8.5M: general operating $1.55M, provincial grant $3.6M, L&B reserve $0.85M, debt $2.5M (minutes R23-252); city share 'just over $30 million' (Siemens, transcript 0:36:13); $5M contingency local improvement By-law 2223 (minutes R23-026/027/169)
reasons: cost: proceeding 5–6 or 20 years earlier would have been cheaper; waiting would not have produced the centre (Jake Hiebert)
notes: Covered more fully in the taxes-spending report.

title: Five-year debt rule kept as the city's long-range financing approach
summary: Members repeatedly defended the policy of repaying every loan within five years, including the event centre loan, as what keeps future councils free to take on new projects. They did not discuss how a much larger future project would be financed under the rule.
status_detail: Rule kept in the 2023 and 2024 budgets. In September 2026 the mayor said he was open to 'creative' longer-term financing for the $215M wastewater system (existing report), which would depart from it.
reasons: cost: shorter terms mean much less interest than 20-year borrowing (Michael Zwaagstra)

title: 2023 financial plan adopted with a short capital outlook
summary: Council adopted the 2023 financial plan ($67.3M capital program, mill rate 13.7, down 2.8%). The public presentation gave only yearly totals for the next four capital years; the largest items named were the event centre, Lift Station 2 and a force main twinning.
status_detail: Adopted unanimously after a public hearing with no public speakers. Only yearly totals of the five-year capital plan were presented.
figures: Capital 2023 $67.3M; 2024 $36.1M; then $22.7M, $26.5M, $19.5M (Hrehirchuk, transcript 0:08:50 and 0:18:59); mill rate 13.7, -2.8% (transcript 0:08:50); new debt just over $12M, all on 5-year terms (transcript 0:12:14)
public: No one spoke at the public hearing.

title: Term priorities cited in public, but no strategic plan tabled
summary: Council's 2022–26 priorities were set in unrecorded Strategic Priorities Committee (SPC) meetings and study sessions. In public, members named them only in passing: infrastructure renewal and expansion, recreation and cultural facility renewal, and regional relationships. No strategic plan document, targets or progress report was tabled at a recorded meeting in 2023–24.
status_detail: Priorities exist as headings. SPC sessions are referred to (Sept 12, 2023 in the transcripts; Feb 13, 2024 in the minutes), but none of the 2023–24 regular meetings adopted or reviewed a written strategic plan.
notes: The priorities list here is assembled from passing remarks; the full 2022–26 list (city relations, enhanced safety, infrastructure renewal and expansion, per the mayor in Mar 2025) was not read out in a 2023–24 meeting.

title: Year-end surpluses moved into reserves for future projects
summary: Approving the 2022 reserve transfers, council moved unplanned surplus into reserves, including about $2.1M to the land and building reserve for 'future requirements' such as the event centre. Development fees brought in about $1.8–1.9M against $615,000 budgeted. Councillor Damian Penner credited staff's 5-, 10- and 20-year capital plans. The 2023 transfers were approved the same way in June 2024.
status_detail: 2022 transfers approved (R23-102); 2023 transfers approved June 18, 2024 (R24-126, S. Penner/Zwaagstra). The 10- and 20-year capital plans mentioned have not been published.
figures: Development fees collected ~$1.8–1.9M vs $615,000 budgeted; environmental reserve +$210,000; land and building reserve transfer ~$2.1M (Warkentin, transcript 0:14:35)

title: Brandt Street lot split denied, partly to keep options open for a corridor plan
summary: Staff recommended denying a small-lot subdivision on Brandt Street (PTH 12) and asked council to weigh long-term impacts. Councillor Siemens agreed, saying council had no long-term plan for the area and should not handicap a future council or a developer assembling land.
status_detail: Subdivision denied unanimously. No long-term plan for the Brandt Street corridor was brought forward in 2023–24.
figures: Proposed lot 31.5 ft wide vs neighbours 82–125 ft (Siemens, transcript 0:23:24)
reasons: market-decides: no firm plan for the area; leave room for a future council or a developer assembling a large lot (Jac Siemens)

title: Downtown business district extended to First Street and PTH 52
summary: Council gave third reading to OCP amendment By-law 2216 after ministerial approval, bringing a First Street / PTH 52 West site into the central business district for a 22–24-unit building. Councillor Siemens voted against at every stage on principle: CBD rules allow near-zero setbacks next to the highway. He and Jake Hiebert also voted against the related lane closing in November.
status_detail: OCP amendment carried 5-1 (July 4, 2023); rezoning By-law 2215 unanimous; lane closing By-law 2232 carried 5-2 (Nov 7, 2023).
figures: 22 to 24 units planned (Warkentin, transcript 2023-07-04 0:19:02)
public: Objections were heard at the 2022 public hearing (outside this period).
mover: Damian Penner (R23-141); Michael Zwaagstra (R23-226); Bill Hiebert (R23-227)
seconder: Jake Hiebert (R23-141); Susan Penner (R23-226); Michael Zwaagstra (R23-227)
vote: 5-1 (against: Jac Siemens); lane closing 5-2 (against: Jac Siemens, Jake Hiebert)
notes: Siemens's July 4 remarks are on a low-confidence speaker label and are not quoted; the minutes record his vote.

title: Economic development office: lack of serviced land is a disadvantage
summary: Steinbach Economic Development (a pilot running 2021–2025) presented its strategy in July 2023, focused on agribusiness, with the mayor and Councillor Susan Penner involved in drafting it. In March 2024 its director told council large manufacturers need serviced land, water and wastewater, and in answer to Councillor Damian Penner called serviced land a disadvantage for Steinbach. Council asked no follow-up and took no action on serviced industrial land in 2023–24.
status_detail: Received as information. No serviced industrial land program or servicing plan was brought to council in 2023–24.
public: M.B. (director, Steinbach Economic Development) said investors want serviced, not just available, land; a large manufacturer lead through the province had not gone further.
notes: M.B. speaks for an organization (the city-funded economic development corporation) and is identified by initials.

title: Support for expanding the Seine-Rat-Roseau Watershed District
summary: Council, already a member, ratified the provincial proposal to expand the Seine Rat Roseau Watershed District (including the RM of Morris). Councillor Jake Hiebert, who reported on the district, said the province has been pushing municipalities to join watersheds.
status_detail: Ratified unanimously; the district's minutes are received regularly as information.

title: Main Street land made public reserve for a future creek-bed pathway
summary: Council created a public reserve at Main Street and Goossen Avenue from city land plus a newly acquired strip, to protect a water line and keep the old Steinbach Creek bed for a future pedestrian corridor.
status_detail: By-law 2229 given third reading Sept 19, 2023. No pathway project or timeline was announced.
seconder: Michael Zwaagstra (1st); Susan Penner (2nd); Bill Hiebert (3rd)
notes: A Sept 5 speaker-map cluster merges two councillors' turns, so those remarks are not quoted.

title: Asset management policy, strategy and plan adopted
summary: Council formally adopted an asset management policy, strategy and plan, discussed earlier at SPC. Staff said a public resolution was a condition of a federal (FCM) asset management grant; members said it puts existing practice in writing and will guide capital planning for 5, 10 and more years.
status_detail: Adopted unanimously. The resolution makes administration responsible for reporting on asset management, but no status report came to a recorded meeting in 2023–24.
notes: The transcript says 'FCA asset management grant'; it is presumably the FCM Municipal Asset Management Program (unverified).

title: Grant sought to renew Hespeler Street ahead of industrial growth
summary: Council applied to the province's new Municipal Economic Development Infrastructure Program for half of a $3.32M Hespeler Street project. Councillor Damian Penner said renewing the industrial corridor before it fills up was 'good foresight'. Applications for Hanover Street and a fire-hall exhaust system went in at the same time.
status_detail: The grant result was not found in 2023–24 minutes or transcripts.
figures: Request $1,660,000 of an estimated $3,320,000 (minutes R23-200)

title: Growth charges raised 5% a year to 2027, not the 7.5% staff recommended
summary: Development fees pay into reserves for growth costs such as lagoon expansion, eventual mechanical wastewater treatment and a second fire station. Staff recommended 7.5% a year for four years to catch up after a decade of 2.5% increases. Council combined three by-laws into By-law 2233 and set 5% a year. Damian Penner and Jake Hiebert voted against, saying 5% leaves existing taxpayers covering more of the cost of growth.
status_detail: By-law 2233 adopted Nov 7, 2023 at 5% a year for 2024–2027, with a review promised for 2027. Staff told council even 7.5% would not cover the cost of growth, and about 11% a year would be needed to restore the earlier contribution level.
figures: Since 2012 fees rose 2.5%/yr vs 5–6%/yr construction inflation (Zwaagstra, transcript 2023-10-17 0:08:47); options presented at SPC: 2.5%, 5%, 7.5%, 10%, with 11% over 4 years needed to catch up (D. Penner, transcript 2023-11-07 0:06:44 and 0:07:13)
reasons: affordability: higher fees are passed on to home buyers; err on the side of affordability because more homes are needed (Michael Zwaagstra); affordability: would not have supported 7.5%; other governments are trying to make housing affordable (Susan Penner); affordability: entry-level housing would be hit hardest; tie the increase to inflation (Mayor Earl Funk); one-step-at-a-time: take a longer-term view; review again in 2027 (Jac Siemens)
seconder: Jac Siemens (1st), Bill Hiebert (2nd), Susan Penner (3rd)
vote: 5-2 at each reading (against: Damian Penner, Jake Hiebert)
notes: Jake Hiebert's speaker label is medium confidence in both meetings, so he is not quoted; his vote is from the minutes.

title: Setback variance on annexed PTH 52 West land denied to protect future development
summary: On a 4-acre property in land annexed from Hanover, council denied a 4-foot side-yard variance for a shed, citing drainage and the precedent it would set for highway-frontage parcels where the city expects to grow west and north.
status_detail: Denied 5-1 (Bill Hiebert against; he did not state a reason).
figures: 15-ft setback required vs 4 ft requested (Warkentin, transcript 0:05:32)
public: The applicant did not attend; no objections were filed.

title: Four-year water and sewer rate plan (2024–2027) adopted
summary: After Public Utilities Board approval, council adopted By-law 2163, setting water and sewer rates for 2024–2027 on a cost-recovery basis, including essential capital upgrades. No new treatment plant or lagoon project was discussed with the rates.
status_detail: Second and third readings Dec 19, 2023, after PUB order 137-23.
figures: Typical residential increase 3–4% a year, 2024–2027 (Warkentin, transcript 0:48:43)

title: Truck yard on city-sold industrial land denied next to homes
summary: A trucking firm bought about 20 acres of M1 industrial land the city had developed in the Hespeler industrial park in the 1990s, next to newer homes. After many residents objected, council unanimously denied the conditional use for a truck yard and a related barbed-wire variance. Members said they wanted the business but could not limit it to the 4 acres first planned.
status_detail: Conditional use CU-2023-02 and variance V-2023-25 denied. The case shows the conflict between remaining industrial land and housing built beside it; no buffer or industrial-land policy change followed in 2024.
figures: 4 acres to be used at first of about 20 acres (Siemens, transcript 1:31:02)
reasons: resident-opposition: a conditional use near many homes faces a higher bar; neighbours raised strong concerns (Michael Zwaagstra)
public: Several nearby residents objected (traffic, noise, safety, water quality). S.U. said the land would be better used for something other than industrial.

title: Holm Street infill: a 4-3 vote on 'growing up, not out'
summary: Rezoning two single-family lots near Bethesda hospital for a three-storey building split council 4-3. Supporters cited downtown vitality and the OCP's aim to grow up, not out; Damian Penner cited a 20-year projection that the population must double and said sprawl would make the city 'fail', yet voted against because of neighbours' opposition. The by-law was referred to the Municipal Board after objections.
status_detail: Second reading carried 4-3; objections sent it to a Municipal Board hearing (Aug 14–16, 2024, R24-159). No third reading appears in the minutes through Oct 2026.
reasons: resident-opposition: well-established single-family area outside the transition zone; neighbours opposed (Michael Zwaagstra); resident-opposition: good location for density, but voted with the neighbours (Damian Penner)
public: Many neighbours objected at the public hearing (character of the block, traffic, construction fatigue); some speakers supported density and walkability. Speakers are not named here.
vote: 4-3 (against: Damian Penner, Jake Hiebert, Michael Zwaagstra)
notes: Also relevant to the housing report.

title: Official Community Plan and zoning by-law rewrite approved for public consultation
summary: The OCP and zoning review began in spring 2023 with consultants. In December 2024 council accepted staff's proposed changes: affordable-housing policies, active transportation links required in new developments, a redrawn central business district around the event centre, a one-third cut in downtown parking requirements, detached secondary suites, and emergency shelters as a conditional use. The zoning by-law was cut from 155 to 106 pages.
status_detail: Direction given to prepare the final by-laws, with public engagement planned for January and hearings in March 2025. The new OCP (By-law 2244) was adopted in September 2025 (existing report).
figures: Zoning by-law 155 → 106 pages; CBD parking requirements cut by one-third (Warkentin, transcript 0:06:35; S. Penner 0:14:32)
notes: The 0:12:51 turn is labelled Susan Penner in the speaker map but is the City Planner (introduced at 0:12:36); it is not quoted. Mayor Funk was absent.

title: 2024 financial plan: 5.1% tax rise, capital outlook as yearly totals
summary: Council adopted the 2024 financial plan and capital plan together ($62.7M capital, mill rate 14.4, up about 5%). Members blamed construction inflation and said they had spread renewal projects into later years. The outlook again showed only yearly totals.
status_detail: Adopted unanimously; no public speakers at the hearing.
figures: Capital 2024 $62.7M; then $20.1M, $5M and $16.1M for the next 3 years (Hrehirchuk, transcript 0:08:30; the $5M year is as transcribed and unverified against the package); mill rate 14.4 (transcript 0:05:52); new debt $16M (transcript 0:08:30)
reasons: cost: renewal projects were spread into upcoming years to hold the increase (Jac Siemens)
public: No one spoke at the public hearing.

title: Roundabout at Loewen and Hespeler: left for the long-term capital plan
summary: A traffic study of Loewen Boulevard and Hespeler Street said more data was needed and a roundabout could be designed in future. A motion for a three-way stop now failed 3-4. The mayor said the best plan was to get a roundabout into the long-term capital plan.
status_detail: Three-way stop to be tried during PTH 12/Loewen construction; no roundabout was added to a published capital plan in 2024.
reasons: study-first: follow the experts; more data and a longer-term picture before changing the intersection (Michael Zwaagstra); one-step-at-a-time: try the 3-way stop during construction, then look again (Mayor Earl Funk)
vote: Defeated 3-4 (for: Jac Siemens, Jake Hiebert, Bill Hiebert; against: Michael Zwaagstra, Damian Penner, Susan Penner, Earl Funk)
notes: Covered more fully in the traffic-congestion report.

title: Twinning the force main to the lagoon: provincial funding sought, engineers hired
summary: To add capacity between Lift Station 1 and the lagoon, council asked the Manitoba Water Services Board to fund half the design, its first use of the board in some time, and hired Associated Engineering for lift station upgrades and force main twinning. This was the only work on lagoon-bound capacity in 2023–24; lagoon capacity and a new treatment plant were not discussed at a recorded meeting.
status_detail: MWSB request June 18 (R24-127); engineering awarded Nov 5 (R24-209) and the amount corrected Nov 19 (R24-223).
figures: Engineering $529,789.89 (R24-209), corrected to $463,201 plus taxes (R24-223); MWSB asked for 50% of design (R24-127)
seconder: Michael Zwaagstra (R24-127); Jac Siemens (R24-209); Damian Penner (R24-223)
notes: The Nov 5, 2024 award has no transcript; the Nov 19 correction was introduced by the City Manager on a mislabelled speaker track and is not quoted.

title: Six-storey mixed-use building on Main Street approved as part of the downtown vision
summary: Council unanimously approved a conditional use and height variance (six storeys, 78 ft) for a commercial-and-residential building at 362–366 Main Street. Every member called it part of a decades-old vision for a denser downtown. The mayor said that vision depends on developers acting.
status_detail: CU-2024-04 and V-2024-04 approved subject to a development agreement.
figures: Six storeys / 78 ft vs 5 storeys / 50 ft allowed (minutes, item 8)
reasons: market-decides: downtown density is developer-driven; council had to wait for a developer (Mayor Earl Funk)

title: Steinbach joins the Eastman Regional Municipal Committee
summary: After Councillor Siemens attended its organizing meeting, council joined the new southern subcommittee of the Eastman Regional Municipal Committee, a lobby group of RMs and towns, for $750 a year, and appointed Siemens. Councillor Susan Penner asked why it was needed alongside AMM, and the mayor worried it could take attention off Steinbach's own needs. Siemens's first asks were highway upgrades and health-care staffing.
status_detail: Joined (R24-170) and Siemens appointed to Dec 31, 2025 (R24-176).
figures: Membership $250 pro-rated for 2024, $750 for 2025 (minutes R24-170)

title: Mayor reports 20 years of growth, but no forward projection
summary: In opening remarks the mayor reported that Steinbach roughly doubled from 2001 to 2021, developers added 1,533 housing units from 2015 to 2022, and $80.5M of infrastructure went into the ground over the same period. No official population forecast was presented in 2023–24; the only forward figure was Damian Penner's mention (March 2024) of a 20-year projection to double the population.
status_detail: No population projection was adopted in 2023–24. The 2025 OCP later projected 34,085 by 2041 (existing report).
figures: Growth 2001–2021 about 93%; 1,533 housing units 2015–2022; $80.5M of infrastructure 2015–2022, city-built and developer-donated (Funk, transcript 0:00:25 and 0:04:29)
notes: The mayor's growth percentages are as transcribed (e.g. '92.983% or 98%') and were not checked against census tables.

title: September 2024 storm overwhelms drainage; disaster aid requested
summary: About 6 inches of rain on Sept 16–17, 2024 filled drains, creeks and ditches beyond capacity, overtopped several streets, washed out 16 gravel-road sections and flooded the T.G. Smith Centre. Several dozen owners reported basement flooding. Council asked the province for Disaster Financial Assistance. No stormwater master plan or drainage review was discussed.
status_detail: DFA request approved Nov 5, 2024 (R24-214). Longer-term drainage planning came only through the FCM climate adaptation application in December 2024.
figures: ~6 inches of rain; flood pump 485 L/s; 16 washouts (Warkentin, transcript 0:26:13 and 0:28:12); 'several dozen' basement floods (minutes 2024-11-05, item 11.2)
notes: The Nov 5, 2024 meeting has no transcript; its update is from the minutes. The sewer-backups report covers basement flooding.

title: Regional library supported in principle; working group joined
summary: Council supported in principle a provincial proposal for a regional library in southeastern Manitoba and named Jac Siemens (alternate Bill Hiebert) to the working group.
status_detail: On Jan 20, 2026 council ended its investigation into regionalization 'as currently proposed by Public Library Services' (R26-009, Siemens/B. Hiebert).
notes: No transcript exists for Nov 5, 2024; the decision is from the minutes.

title: Grant application for a climate risk assessment and adaptation plan
summary: Council applied to FCM's Local Leadership for Climate Adaptation initiative, which would pay 70% of consultants' costs for a climate risk assessment and adaptation plan. Members presented it as a funding opportunity: Siemens called it federal 'downloading', and Zwaagstra said it would help future grant applications. A month earlier Zwaagstra had said residents care about safe water more than climate emergency resolutions.
status_detail: Application approved unanimously. The resulting plan was presented in August 2026 and had not been adopted as of October 2026 (existing report).
figures: FCM would fund 70% of project costs (Thiessen, transcript 0:50:52)
reasons: provincial-responsibility: climate work is being downloaded by the federal government to communities (Jac Siemens); waiting-for-funding: worth doing mainly because outside funding pays most of it and it helps future grant applications (Michael Zwaagstra); basics-first: essential services before climate resolutions (Nov 2024 opening remarks) (Michael Zwaagstra)
notes: Mayor Funk was absent on Dec 3, 2024.

title: Objection to an RM of Hanover rezoning in the transition zone north of the city
summary: Hanover approved a subdivision just north of city limits on PTH 12 over Steinbach's objection, issued building permits, then proposed rezoning it rural industrial. Council objected, saying this breaks Hanover's own development plan, provincial policy, the 2018 joint highway access plan and the annexation agreement, and fragments land Steinbach may need.
status_detail: Objection filed for Hanover's Jan 8, 2025 hearing. The outcome is outside this period and was not verified. Steinbach has no joint fringe-area plan with Hanover.
reasons: neighbours-disagree: the city's interests differ from Hanover's; protect land for future growth (Michael Zwaagstra)

title: Force main twinning and Lift Station 1 upgrade approved as the first step toward wastewater expansion
summary: Council held the public hearing on Local Improvement Plan 2025-01 (By-law 2255) to twin the 3 km sewage force main from Lift Station 1 on Park Road West to the lagoon, gave it three readings, and asked the Manitoba Water Services Board (MWSB) for 50% of the cost. Members described it as the first step before a larger lagoon/treatment expansion.
status_detail: By-law 2255 received third reading July 2, 2025. MWSB confirmed a $3,650,000 grant (reported Aug 19, 2025; minutes say the project had been in the long-term capital plan since 2021). Construction contracts followed in 2026 (see 2026-wastewater-capacity-contracts).
figures: Total $6.595M; borrowing up to $2.75M over 5 years at max 7%, ~0.488 mills, just under $50/yr on a $250,000 home (transcript Feb 4, 2025, 0:05:25); MWSB grant $3,650,000 (minutes Aug 19, 2025, item 6.1).
reasons: already-planned: Twinning was planned when the line was built ~30 years ago; growth now requires it (speaker identification medium). (Bill Hiebert)
public: No residents spoke or wrote at the Feb 4, 2025 public hearing (transcript 0:05:25: 'There is no written correspondence on the file').
mover: Susan Penner (1st), Jac Siemens (2nd; MWSB request), Michael Zwaagstra (3rd)
seconder: Jac Siemens (1st), Bill Hiebert (2nd), Jake Hiebert (MWSB request), Susan Penner (3rd)
notes: Bill Hiebert's quote rests on a medium-confidence speaker map (label C, 2025-02-04).

title: Financial plans keep a 7–10-year capital look-ahead and the five-year debt rule
summary: The 2025 and 2026 financial plans each published a capital program plus three further years of estimated totals, with a spike in years 3–4 for the wastewater work. A resident asked at the 2025 hearing how the city knows it is not falling behind on infrastructure; the city manager said the city keeps a 7–10-year look-ahead (more than the provincial 5) and uses engineering models and pavement ratings. Council kept the rule of repaying all debt within five years.
status_detail: Both plans adopted unanimously with a 14.4-mill municipal rate. Only yearly totals of the look-ahead were presented in public; no itemized long-range plan or asset-condition report was tabled.
reasons: already-planned: Staff keep a 7–10-year capital document and engineering models. (Troy Warkentin, City Manager); cost: Longer-term debt would lower payments now but cost more in taxes overall. (Michael Zwaagstra)
public: G.S. (Mar 4, 2025) noted the book value of city infrastructure declined 2010–2022 and asked what measures ensure the city isn't falling behind 'without burdening future generations'. D.J. (Jul 21, 2026) said Steinbach 'has at times planned for growth before ensuring the necessary infrastructure was in place', citing Clear Spring Greens (resident's view).
seconder: Susan Penner (2025 in principle), Bill Hiebert (2025 final), Susan Penner (2026)
notes: Hrehirchuk's 2026 presentation is on label D (2026-03-17), mapped high; the same label also carries a councillor's remarks at 0:47:52, which are not used.

title: 2022–26 strategic priorities cited as four headings; no published plan, and none yet for 2026–30
summary: Asked about long-term infrastructure, the mayor listed the term's strategic priorities, set in 2022: city relations, enhanced safety, infrastructure renewal and expansion, and recreation and cultural facility renewal. Infrastructure renewal was repeatedly called a 'core value'. Priority-setting happens at unrecorded Strategic Priority Committee meetings and study sessions (e.g. the Nov 2025 flood-mitigation study session; an Aug 11, 2026 SPC meeting).
status_detail: No strategic plan document with goals, timelines or measures was tabled at a recorded meeting in 2025–26. The new council's Nov 3, 2026 inaugural meeting dealt only with oaths and appointments; 2026–30 priorities had not been set publicly.
notes: Minutes of Jul 21, 2026 (item 44) record a decision deferred 'until a Strategic Priority Committee meeting could be held on August 11, 2026' — those meetings are not recorded.

title: New Official Community Plan (By-law 2244) adopted with a 25–30-year horizon
summary: After a review begun in 2023 with WSP, council held the public hearing on April 1, 2025, gave first and second readings, and gave third reading on Sept 16, 2025 after the minister approved the plan without amendment despite objections, some from adjacent municipalities. Members described it as a long-term guide: growth 'up and out', downtown densification, infill, active transportation, industrial land, and a ban on private wells where city water is available.
status_detail: By-law 2244 in force from Sept 16, 2025, replacing By-law 2099 (2018). The plan projects population to 2041 (per the published OCP, external) but no population or land figures were discussed at the hearing; the mayor confirmed the city had no survey of residents' awareness of the plan.
figures: Planning horizon 25–30 years (City Planner, Apr 1, 2025, 0:06:32); 3 written objections at hearing (minutes Apr 1, 2025); OCP projects 34,085 residents by 2041 (published OCP, external).
public: A.A. asked how many residents even know about the plan and whether the city had a survey (Apr 1, 2025, 0:30:12–0:31:15); L.D. (for a transitional-housing board) asked about emergency-shelter rules. Three objections were filed; adjacent municipalities also objected to the minister (Sept 16, 2025, 1:01:13).
mover: Jac Siemens (1st), Jake Hiebert (2nd), Susan Penner (3rd)
seconder: Michael Zwaagstra (1st), Bill Hiebert (2nd), Michael Zwaagstra (3rd)
notes: Michael Zwaagstra's Apr 1, 2025 OCP remarks (0:51:14) are on a merged staff/councillor label (medium) and are not quoted. The adjacent municipalities that objected were not named at the meeting.

title: New Zoning By-law 2245 enacted after a Municipal Board review
summary: The zoning by-law that implements the OCP received first and second readings on April 1, 2025. Objections sent it to the Municipal Board (council delegated the city manager and planner to the October 2025 hearing); the Board ordered no changes and council gave third reading on January 20, 2026. Changes include a one-third cut in required parking, a central business district overlay and emergency shelters as a conditional use.
status_detail: By-law 2245 enacted Jan 20, 2026; a first amendment (By-law 2275) followed in Apr–Jun 2026.
figures: Required parking reduced by one-third for all uses (Zwaagstra, Jan 20, 2026, 0:29:47).
public: Objections at the April 1, 2025 hearing (several on emergency shelters) triggered the Municipal Board hearing.
mover: Susan Penner (1st), Jac Siemens (2nd; Municipal Board delegation), Michael Zwaagstra (3rd)
seconder: Damian Penner (1st), Jake Hiebert (2nd, 3rd), Bill Hiebert (delegation)

title: City signs the Eastman Regional Municipal Committee MOU for joint lobbying
summary: Council approved an MOU with the Eastman Regional Municipal Committee (Southern Sub-Committee), a group of south-eastern municipalities (11 in Apr 2025, 16 by Jun 2026) lobbying the province on highways, health care, drainage and water. Jac Siemens reported that it raised threats to the Sandilands aquifer, Steinbach's water source, from water co-ops seeking to draw on it.
status_detail: MOU approved; regular reports followed (Sept 2025, June 2026). On Nov 3, 2026 the mayor appointed Councillor Jake Hiebert as the city's ERMC representative.
figures: 11 member municipalities (Apr 2025), 12 (Sept 2025), 16 (Jun 2026) (Siemens, transcripts).

title: $132.5M wastewater treatment expansion: federal funding application, and the regional co-op option rejected
summary: Council ratified an application to the federal Canada Housing Infrastructure Fund for 50% of a $132.5M project: a new or expanded wastewater treatment facility, primary lift station and second force main, and a west-end lift station and gravity main to service about 2 square miles of unserviced land. Staff explained that, after a joint study, the city chose its own plant over joining the Red-Seine-Rat (RSR) wastewater co-op, which was estimated at 25–30% more and would have required ceding ownership of lagoon land.
status_detail: Application ratified unanimously. No funding decision was reported at any recorded council meeting through Nov 3, 2026; by 2026 members cited costs over $200M (see 2026-wastewater-cost-rise). Staff said a further application to the joint federal–provincial CHIF stream was being prepared.
figures: Eligible cost $132,475,000; city commits to the balance of $65,447,500 (minutes R25-081). Components: treatment ~$94M; force main/lift station ~$8M; west lift station + 1.5 km gravity main ~$30M (Warkentin, 0:15:25). RSR option 25–30% costlier (same).
reasons: cost: RSR co-op option estimated 25–30% more expensive than a city-only plant. (Troy Warkentin, City Manager); local-control: Joining the co-op would mean ceding ownership of city facilities; 'the city have control over our own facilities'. (Michael Zwaagstra); waiting-for-funding: Project depends on substantial support from other governments; applying 'long in advance'. (Michael Zwaagstra)
notes: Members gave different capacity horizons in 2025: 5 years (mayor), 5–6 years (Bill Hiebert, Feb 4), 7–8 years (Siemens). The RSR comparison study was completed in spring 2024 and council consensus was reached then in an unrecorded session; the public record is this Apr 15, 2025 explanation.

title: First Active Transportation Plan accepted as a long-term plan 'in principle'
summary: Council accepted the city's first consultant-prepared Active Transportation Plan (Urban Systems): a long-term network of mostly off-road multi-use paths, shared streets and Share the Road routes. Members welcomed a proactive plan but stressed it is a plan in principle, that the full network (about $11M) will not happen soon, and that it must not impede car travel.
status_detail: Accepted unanimously. No multi-year implementation budget or schedule was adopted at a recorded meeting; members expected low-cost items (signage, Share the Road) first.
figures: Full network about $11M (Zwaagstra, 1:03:48).
reasons: cost: Price tags are very high; most of the plan is 'significantly in the future'. (Michael Zwaagstra); one-step-at-a-time: Do some things every year and 'whittle away at it'. (Mayor Earl Funk); vehicles-first: Active transportation must not hinder vehicle traffic; sidewalks in established areas draw opposition. (Michael Zwaagstra)

title: Climate risk assessment and adaptation plan: funded 2025, presented Aug 2026, not adopted
summary: Council funded a climate adaptation and mitigation plan in the 2025 budget, supported by an FCM Green Municipal Fund grant of up to $70,000. After the Sept 2025 storm, Susan Penner urged fast-tracking it and the mayor promised a 'roadmap of projects' by spring 2026. WSP presented the climate risk assessment and adaptation plan on Aug 18, 2026, stressing it is a planning document, 'not a commitment to implement every action immediately'.
status_detail: Plan delivered about four months late (Aug 18, 2026) and received; no adoption or funding of its actions appears in minutes through Oct 6, 2026 or the Oct 20 / Nov 3, 2026 transcripts. The city manager said the study would be made public.
figures: FCM Green Municipal Fund grant up to $70,000 (minutes Jul 2, 2025, item 16); 1-in-100-year-plus storms in Sept 2024 (95.9 mm) and Sept 2025 (~126 mm in 4 hours) (Warkentin, Sept 16, 2025, 0:41:04).
reasons: study-first: Projects will be chosen once the climate plan gives a roadmap. (Mayor Earl Funk); waiting-for-funding: Federal climate programs 'often also come with funding'. (Mayor Earl Funk)
public: Flood-affected residents asked repeatedly (Oct 2025, Mar 2026) for studies explaining why their neighbourhoods flooded.
notes: The Aug 18, 2026 presentation has no transcript; its content is from the minutes (items 6–6.6).

title: City defends its objection to an RM of Hanover fringe rezoning at the Municipal Board
summary: Following its Dec 2024 objection to RM of Hanover rezoning By-law 2578-24 near the city boundary (to protect land Steinbach may annex), council delegated the city manager and city planner to represent the city at the Municipal Board hearing set for Aug 22/25, 2025.
status_detail: Delegation approved; the Board's decision was not reported at any recorded meeting found.
reasons: neighbours-disagree: Rural development at the edge would compromise future annexation (stated Dec 2024; prior period). (Council)
notes: No transcript for Aug 19, 2025; minutes only.

title: Outdoor pool renewal: long-planned facility work sent to the province for 50% funding
summary: Council applied to Manitoba's Growth, Renewal and Opportunities (GROW) program for half of the outdoor pool renewal, a project staff said had sat on the long-term capital program for 10–12 years for lack of recreation funding. It applied again in October 2026 at a higher estimate.
status_detail: Applications made Sept 2025 (R25-182) and Oct 20, 2026; no funding result reported at a recorded meeting.
reasons: waiting-for-funding: Hard to find funding sources that fit recreation projects. (Troy Warkentin, City Manager)

title: Council asks the province to raise the Manitoba Water Services Board budget to $100M
summary: Council endorsed a Manitoba Municipal Administrators' resolution asking the province to raise MWSB capital funding to $100M a year, after hearing that $24M was available against $1.35B in 2024 requests. Members said growth stops without water and wastewater capacity.
status_detail: Resolution passed unanimously and forwarded; no provincial response was reported at a recorded meeting.
figures: MWSB funding $24M available vs $1.35B applied for in 2024; 50/50 cost sharing so ~$48M of projects/year; 103 municipalities' projects unfunded (mayor and Susan Penner, Oct 7, 2025, 0:28:38–0:28:55).
reasons: provincial-responsibility: Smaller cities cannot afford projects of this size without provincial help. (Susan Penner)

title: Protecting the aquifer: comments on Sio Silica's sand-mining licence; joint response revisited
summary: When Sio Silica re-applied for an Environment Act licence for silica sand extraction wells, council directed staff to submit comments by Dec 1, 2025, with members calling water the most important resource and noting the city draws on the same aquifer as about 12 municipalities. In May 2026, asked by the RM of Ste. Anne to back a resolution and reconvene the joint action committee, council instead asked staff to reconnect with the former committee municipalities; the mayor said the resolution's extra regulation would add costs.
status_detail: Comments authorized (R25-230); May 5, 2026 matter referred to administration to report back — no report found at a recorded meeting by Nov 3, 2026. No long-term water supply study was presented in the period.
figures: About 12 municipalities draw on the aquifer (mayor, Nov 18, 2025, 1:13:55); comment deadline Dec 1, 2025.
reasons: cost: Declined to back Ste. Anne's resolution: more regulation would add costs; Manitoba already strict. (Mayor Earl Funk)
notes: Nov 4, 2025 remarks by a Hiebert (label C, low confidence) urging a joint objection with other municipalities are not quoted.

title: Record growth and competing population projections (36,936 by 2045 vs 44,000 by 2046)
summary: Council celebrated record years: 365 dwelling units in 2025 and over $112M in permits, then a record 148 units in August 2026. Members cited different current populations (20,011 vs 22,000) and different 20-year projections (36,936 by 2045 vs 44,000 by 2046). Jac Siemens credited the 2018 Hanover annexation with securing 40–50 years of land. The mayor said a fast-growing city will need 'a really strong council'.
status_detail: No single official population forecast was adopted or presented at a recorded meeting; council did not discuss what the projections mean for services beyond wastewater.
figures: 2025: 365 dwelling units (mayor, Jan 20, 2026, 0:31:51); ~$112M permits (Jake Hiebert, Dec 16, 2025, 1:11:36); Aug 2026: 148 units, $25M residential (Susan Penner, Sept 15, 2026, 0:52:16); population 20,011 (2025) → 36,936 (2045) (mayor, Apr 21, 2026); 22,000 → 44,000 (2046) (Siemens, Mar 17, 2026); city area 25.6 → ~38 km² after 2018 annexation (Siemens).
reasons: growth-unpredictable: 'we don't know when it's going to end or if it's ever going to end' (Sept 15, 2026). (Mayor Earl Funk)
notes: The Municipal Board in 2017–18 approved the annexation as roughly a 30-year supply (prior-period source cited in the existing report), shorter than Siemens' 40–50 years.

title: 2026 sewer capacity contracts: Park Road West force main, Millwork Drive main and Lift Station 1
summary: Council asked MWSB for 50% of the Millwork Drive sewer main (Dec 2025) and in early 2026 awarded three contracts that staff said had been on the long-term capital plan since 2022: the Park Road West force main, the Millwork Drive sewer main renewal (larger pipe for growth, 75–100 year life) and the Lift Station 1 upgrade that nearly doubles pumping capacity.
status_detail: All three contracts awarded unanimously (Feb 17, Mar 3 and Mar 17, 2026) at or below engineers' estimates; construction scheduled for 2026. Members also tied the work to the 2024–25 basement flooding.
figures: Force main $1,494,661.05 vs engineer's estimate $2.4M; overall Park Road West project est. $7.4M (Damian Penner, Feb 17, 2026, 0:28:26); Millwork Drive $1,462,540 vs estimate $2,129,607; Lift Station 1 $4,326,078.39, capacity 482 → 843 L/s (transcripts; minutes R26-038, R26-050, R26-060).
reasons: already-planned: Council placed these projects on the long-term capital plan beginning in 2022, before the storms (Mar 17, 2026, 0:17:48). (Troy Warkentin, City Manager)
public: Residents of flood-affected neighbourhoods (e.g. M.R.) asked at the 2026 budget hearing for studies explaining the root cause of sewer backups; council pointed to these projects.
mover: Susan Penner (R25-258, R26-038), Damian Penner (R26-050), Michael Zwaagstra (R26-060)
seconder: Jake Hiebert (R25-258), Damian Penner (R26-038), Michael Zwaagstra (R26-050), Jac Siemens (R26-060)

title: Wastewater project cost passes $200M; council looks to senior governments and regulators
summary: In 2026 council members described the coming wastewater treatment project as the biggest investment in city history, with projected costs 'over $200 million'. Susan Penner urged council to challenge provincial environmental requirements and approval processes that drive cost; Jac Siemens reported federal infrastructure funding for 'our lagoon' as the top topic at FCM.
status_detail: No funding agreement, final design or financing plan was presented at a recorded meeting through Nov 3, 2026. Per SteinbachOnline (Sept 2026) the mayor called the ~$215M system his top priority for the new term, expecting a three-way split leaving the city ~$72M (external; not stated at a recorded meeting).
figures: 'over $200 million' (Susan Penner, May 5, 2026, 0:00:12); 'about $130 million' in Oct 2025 (Susan Penner, Oct 7, 2025, 0:30:40); $215M / ~$72M city share (SteinbachOnline, Sept 2026, external).
reasons: provincial-responsibility: Provincial over-regulation and approval processes are driving infrastructure costs; council should push for outcome-based regulation. (Susan Penner); waiting-for-funding: Access to federal funding for major projects like the lagoon is the key question. (Jac Siemens)
notes: Susan Penner says 'water treatment facility/plant' on May 5, 2026; in context she means the wastewater facility.

title: City buys 6.7 acres beside the landfill 'for future municipal purposes'
summary: Council bought 148 Hanover Road East (6.7 acres with a 5,400 sq ft shop), next to the landfill, for $450,000 from the environmental reserve, for interim city use until needed for landfill expansion. Michael Zwaagstra compared it to the decades of downtown land buying that later made the Event Centre possible.
status_detail: Purchase approved; possession June 18, 2026. In Oct 2026 council also replaced the landfill compactor early, partly to extend the landfill's life (Oct 20, 2026 transcript).
figures: $450,000; 6.7 acres; from the environmental reserve fund, no mill-rate impact (minutes R26-010; Zwaagstra 0:20:12).

title: City ends talks on a south-eastern Manitoba regional library
summary: After a Public Library Services working group of 10 municipalities met six times in 2025, council voted to end its participation in the regional library process as proposed and keep the Jake Epp (J-CAP) library operating as is. Reasons: most municipalities had already said no, a 2023 provincial funding formula now requires six municipalities, unclear costs, and loss of local autonomy. Members said the door stays open.
status_detail: Carried unanimously; no regional library. 'No for now, but it's not no forever' (mayor).
figures: 10 of 18 invited municipalities joined the working group; 8 later said no; regional advantage now needs 6 municipalities; ~$10 per capita plus building costs for small RMs (Siemens, 0:05:04 and 0:13:29).
reasons: neighbours-disagree: Most municipalities said no before it reached council. (Michael Zwaagstra); provincial-responsibility: Province's 2023 funding formula makes regionalization unworkable. (Michael Zwaagstra); local-control: Did not want the library to lose its autonomy. (Mayor Earl Funk); cost: Unknown financial implications for the city and library. (Jac Siemens)
notes: Member stances refer to the regional library proposal (all voted to end the talks). Label D on 2026-01-20 is a merged Siemens/Bill Hiebert cluster (medium); the Siemens quote is rated high because the chair addressed him immediately before and the minutes name him as mover.

title: Post-storm drainage program: Land Drainage By-law, 2026 projects and possible drainage master plan
summary: After two extreme storms, council used a Nov 2025 study session to set a flood-mitigation program: 2026 drainage projects (PTH 52 East, Park Road East), rerouting the Clear Spring Greens low-pressure sewer, and a new Land Drainage By-law 2274 (replacing the sump pump by-law) with inspections and fines. Staff listed further possible work, including a master plan for drainage catchment areas, a basement-depth policy review and a major drain bypass or detention concept.
status_detail: By-law 2274 enacted Aug 4, 2026 and 2026 projects budgeted; the drainage catchment master plan and other studies were described only as possible future projects.
figures: Annual programs: sanitary sewer televising ~$100,000, storm sewer ~$60,000, major drains $50,000 (Warkentin, Mar 17, 2026, 0:17:48).
reasons: study-first: Further projects depend on consultant studies and the climate risk assessment. (Troy Warkentin, City Manager)
public: Residents (M.R., D.J. and others) asked council to show engineering evidence that infrastructure can handle growth before approving density.
mover: Jake Hiebert (1st), Michael Zwaagstra (2nd), Damian Penner (3rd)
seconder: Michael Zwaagstra (1st), Jake Hiebert (2nd), Bill Hiebert (3rd)
notes: A separate report covers sewer backups in detail; this entry records only the long-range planning pieces.

title: No objection to Town of Ste. Anne annexation; mayor backs growth around urban centres
summary: Municipal Board notice of a proposed annexation of RM of Ste. Anne land by the Town of Ste. Anne was received as information. The mayor said it fits council's policy preference for densifying and growing urban centres rather than fragmented rural development.
status_detail: Received as information; council raised no objection (deadline Apr 20, 2026).

title: City takes over the Manning Canal from the province (MOU)
summary: Council approved an MOU with Manitoba Transportation and Infrastructure to transfer jurisdiction over the parts of the Manning Canal inside city limits, the only drain in Steinbach still under provincial control, first requested in 2022. Members said city control will speed drainage improvements and development along it, including planned detention ponds.
status_detail: MOU approved; the formal transfer needs a provincial order-in-council. By Aug 4, 2026 the city was approving a plan of works to rebuild a canal section for the Williams Creek subdivision.

title: Council objects to RM of La Broquerie plan that would drop the transitional area at Steinbach's edge
summary: La Broquerie's five-year development plan review and zoning by-law proposed removing the 'transitional policy area' within 2 miles of Steinbach and allowing more rural development, including two-unit dwellings, on rural services. Staff found inconsistencies with provincial land use policy; council voted to object to protect land it may annex for future growth.
status_detail: Objection filed before La Broquerie's Sept 23, 2026 hearing; the outcome rests with La Broquerie and the province and was not reported by Nov 3, 2026. On Nov 3 the mayor appointed Councillor Greg Carlos to the Steinbach–La Broquerie Joint Action Committee.
figures: Transitional policy area: development within 2 miles of the city (staff report read at 0:47:43).
reasons: neighbours-disagree: Rural development next to Deerfield would block future annexation. (Bill Hiebert); growth-unpredictable: 'we don't know when it's going to end'; land once developed can't be redeveloped for the city. (Mayor Earl Funk)

title: New council's first acts: Joint Action Committees with Hanover and La Broquerie, ERMC and watershed seats
